README.md.overview: The README is the front door of the project and the best single source for a two-minute pitch. It covers the whole system: seven TF-IDF baselines plus FinBERT (zero-shot and fine-tuned), stratified CV and GridSearchCV, an honest out-of-domain test on real news with bootstrap intervals, the LangChain LLM benchmark and RAG page, the FastAPI service, the Streamlit dashboard and four deployment options. It is the main reference for tour step 1, and its later sections preview most of the other tour steps. A theme that runs through it is honesty: synthetic data, chance-level stock results and in-domain vs out-of-domain caveats are all stated openly.

sections.title: Title and live demo
sections.explanation: The one-line tagline sums up the project: 7 baselines plus FinBERT, honest OOD evaluation with bootstrap CIs, SHAP, FastAPI and Streamlit. The live-demo URL is still a placeholder (`<your-app>.streamlit.app`), and the interview guide's readiness checklist lists filling it in as a to-do. Screenshots show the Home page, where every score is drawn with its 95% interval, which reflects the UI's 'report with uncertainty' design.

sections.title: Overview and key features
sections.explanation: The 'What Makes This Project Stand Out' table is a ready-made answer to 'pitch this project'. It goes models, LLM engineering, ML rigor, explainability, generalization, dashboard, CI/CD and deployment. Note the headline arc in the Generalization row: TF-IDF 0.46 macro-F1 out of domain becomes 0.84 after FinBERT is fine-tuned on news. The feature list labels the synthetic headlines and the chance-level LSTM as demonstrations, not evidence. Interviewers tend to reward that kind of candour.

sections.title: Architecture, structure and setup
sections.explanation: A Mermaid flowchart shows the layers: data (preprocess.py), training (train.py for baselines, model.py for transformers), explainability, cross-dataset validation, the predict.py inference engine and the Streamlit pages. The key path is PhraseBank -> processed splits -> saved models -> evaluate.py -> results/ JSON, which the UI reads instead of recomputing. The project tree and the install/run commands (Makefile, `train.py --model all|cv|tune`, `finetune_finbert_news.py`) map each CLI entry point to a module, which helps if you are asked to walk through how you would reproduce a number.

sections.title: Datasets and model tables
sections.explanation: PhraseBank AllAgree: 2,264 sentences, 61% neutral, stratified 80/10/10 with seed 42. The synthetic headlines are explicitly flagged as not real. The baseline table puts test scores (n=226) next to 5-fold CV macro-F1 and says plainly that the small test set makes single numbers indicative (about +/-3-4%). That is why SVM is the default even though Gradient Boosting has the higher test score: under CV they are tied (0.838 vs 0.835) and SVM is faster.

sections.title: Cross-validation and tuning
sections.explanation: Documents the 5-fold stratified CV run on train+val (2,033 samples) and the GridSearchCV setup, both scored on macro-F1. The CV table is the evidence for choosing SVM. The tuning table lists the SVM C grid and the 18 Gradient Boosting combinations. These numbers come from `cross_validate_baselines` and `tune_hyperparameters` in src/train.py, so you can point straight to that code.

sections.title: Generalization on real news
sections.explanation: This is the central finding: the PhraseBank-trained SVM falls to 0.67 accuracy and 0.46 macro-F1 on 2,388 real headlines, barely above the 0.66 majority baseline. Fine-tuning on news recovers it (DistilBERT 0.73, FinBERT 0.84). The section is careful to say that for the fine-tuned models the validation split is in-domain held-out data, not OOD. It also admits a small optimistic bias, because the best epoch is chosen on the first 500 rows of that same split. Raise both caveats yourself before an interviewer does.

sections.title: LLM benchmark, RAG and explainability
sections.explanation: Describes the Claude/OpenRouter/OpenAI setup through environment variables. The benchmark design uses Pydantic Literal structured output, invalid answers scored as wrong, few-shot examples taken only from the PhraseBank training split, the shared bootstrap and a disk cache. Result: Claude Haiku zero-shot reaches 0.792 macro-F1 against FinBERT's 0.841, with non-overlapping CIs, and loses mainly on neutral headlines. The RAG description explains why embeddings are local TF-IDF+LSA (Anthropic has no embeddings API) and how citations are validated. Later subsections cover the synthetic pipeline demo and the theory behind TF-IDF, the model families and SHAP.

sections.title: Dashboard, CLI and testing
sections.explanation: Lists each dashboard page with its purpose, gives a CLI reference for training, evaluation, prediction and explainability, and summarises the test suite and CI. Watch the test counts: this section says 88 tests across 8 files, while the Q&A and the interview guide say 147. The section has probably not been updated, so quote the current figure from the guide or from a pytest run.

sections.title: API, monitoring and deployment
sections.explanation: Documents the FastAPI endpoints and the hardening you can configure through environment variables: optional X-API-Key auth, Pydantic length and batch limits, slowapi rate limits with optional Redis, and a JSONL audit trail. It then covers the SHA-256 model registry, the monthly retraining that requires human review, and four deployment options. The scaled option is worth knowing well: the UI turns into a stateless RemotePredictor client when FINSIGHT_API_URL is set, nginx balances across API replicas, and Redis keeps rate limits global.

sections.title: Tech stack, Q&A and limitations
sections.explanation: Ends with a technology table, prepared interview answers and a limitations table. Some answers are out of date: the 'more time' answer proposes DistilBERT fine-tuning, which is already done, and the limitations table says OOD generalization is 'not yet measured', which the generalization section contradicts. An interviewer reading the repo might notice these, so know the current story (0.90 -> 0.46 -> 0.84) and be ready to say the docs lag behind the code in places.

docs/INTERVIEW_GUIDE.md.overview: A preparation guide written for exactly this use: likely interview questions with answers that point to specific files. It covers the pitch, architecture, data, models, evaluation, explainability, serving, testing, challenges, limitations, trade-offs, scaling, ethics, a demo script, a question bank and a numbers cheat sheet. It supports tour step 1 and gives the headline result to remember: 0.90 in-domain, 0.46 on real news, 0.84 after fine-tuning. Its own rule applies throughout: only claim what you can defend at a whiteboard.

sections.title: Purpose and readiness checklist
sections.explanation: States the rule for using the guide: every answer points to a file, so open that file before the interview. The checklist separates completed work (CI green, 147 tests, bootstrap CIs, documented limitations) from open tasks (deploy and fill in the URL, record a demo GIF, warm up the sleeping free-tier app, run the LLM benchmark). It also says to read sections 11 and 12 twice, because challenges and limitations are where interviews are decided.

sections.title: Pitch and problem framing
sections.explanation: The core message is that you tested on real data, found the failure, diagnosed it and fixed it: 0.90 -> 0.46 -> 0.84. The 2-minute version follows a clear arc: problem, data (61% neutral, hence macro-F1), baselines with CV, stress test, SHAP diagnosis (stopwords among the top features), FinBERT fix, production hardening, LLM layer. The motivation part explains why finance sentiment is hard: domain vocabulary like 'liability', sentiment carried by numbers, neutral dominance and domain shift.

sections.title: Architecture and prediction path
sections.explanation: An ASCII diagram separates offline work (preprocess, train, evaluate, registry) from online serving (Streamlit in-process, or a split mode through nginx and FastAPI replicas). The 'path of a single prediction' paragraph explains how SentimentPredictor routes requests: TF-IDF pipeline, voting ensemble stored as {tfidf, ensemble}, or transformer. Its design-decision list (one predictor interface, results as JSON artifacts, optional UI/API split, `@st.cache_resource`) gives good answers to 'why is it built this way?'.

sections.title: Data choices
sections.explanation: Summarises PhraseBank AllAgree (2,264 sentences, 16 annotators) and the MIT-licensed news set, whose training split was used only for fine-tuning. It explains the cleaning rules: numbers and the symbols % $ - + are kept because they carry financial meaning, and stopwords are deliberately not removed. The likely questions cover the AllAgree trade-off (cleaner labels but easier sentences, which inflates in-domain scores) and leakage (de-duplicate before splitting, and use the test split only for final scoring).

sections.title: Model choices and recipes
sections.explanation: Lists the exact TF-IDF settings and classifier hyperparameters from train.py, and explains why the SVM is calibrated inside the soft-voting ensemble: LinearSVC has no predict_proba. The FinBERT fine-tuning table (AdamW at 2e-5, 10% warmup, class weights, gradient clipping, AMP, best-epoch restore, patience 2) matches model.py. The Q&A defends the main choices: start with fast, explainable baselines, prefer FinBERT for its domain pre-training, use warmup to protect pre-trained weights, and keep to few epochs because BERT overfits quickly.

sections.title: Evaluation and explainability
sections.explanation: Explains why macro-F1 matters here: always predicting neutral gives 0.61 accuracy but only 0.25 macro-F1. It orders the evidence from weakest to strongest: single split, CV, bootstrap CIs, OOD test. The intervals show the top baselines are statistically tied on n=226, while SVM and FinBERT on news do not overlap. The explainability table separates exact linear attributions, SHAP, lexicons and the rule-based 'reasoning', and notes that the reasoning is not an LLM.

sections.title: Serving, UX and testing
sections.explanation: Covers the API guards (Pydantic validation, opt-in API key, slowapi with Redis so N replicas do not allow N times the rate), the operations tooling (monitoring, SHA-256 registry, manual promotion of retrained models) and the deployment setups. The UX section explains the persistent sidebar router and showing uncertainty everywhere. The testing section explains the strategy: test deterministic code and invariants thoroughly, and guard model quality with evaluation thresholds rather than unit tests.

sections.title: Challenges, limitations, trade-offs
sections.explanation: Eight situation-action-result stories, including the DeBERTa fp16/fp32 crash, Git LFS pointer files on the host, a retraining job that failed silently, an IGNORECASE regex bug, the ProsusAI label order left in config.json, and an LLM 'score' that was really HTTP 402 errors. The limitations table pairs each weakness with a fix. The trade-offs table and the scaling notes (stateless replicas, dynamic batching, caching, queue-based batch jobs) prepare you for system-design follow-up questions.

sections.title: Ethics, demo, question bank, numbers
sections.explanation: Security and responsible-use points: input caps, HTML escaping, pinned dependencies, not financial advice, a human in the loop for uncertain predictions, and dataset licences (PhraseBank is non-commercial). Then come the live demo script, short definitions for rapid-fire questions, STAR-format behavioural answers and the numbers cheat sheet (memorise it). The code walkthrough map gives the file order to open if asked to 'show me the code': predict.py, train.py, model.py, bootstrap_ci.py, api/main.py.

sections.title: LLM benchmark and RAG
sections.explanation: Explains how the LLM comparison is kept fair: same 2,388 headlines, same bootstrap code in stats.py, few-shot examples from PhraseBank train only, temperature 0, and a versioned prompt that is part of the cache key. It also explains the robustness measures: Literal-typed structured output, invalid answers counted as wrong, and failed calls not cached. For RAG it justifies the in-memory store and local LSA embeddings, describes how citations are validated against what was retrieved, and covers the prompt-injection guard and how both features are tested with stubs and no API key.

docs/PRD.md.overview: A short product requirements document that frames the project as a product rather than a notebook: who it is for, what it must do and, just as important, what it must not claim. It supports tour step 1 by answering 'what problem does it solve and for whom?'. Its non-goals explain why the rest of the codebase is so careful to label the stock extension and the template-based explanations honestly.

sections.title: Problem, users, goals, non-goals
sections.explanation: The problem is that financial text is dense and time-sensitive, so the product turns it into a sentiment signal with an explanation. The target users openly include interviewers and students alongside analysts, which tells you this is a portfolio project. The non-goals do the most work: no claim of predicting stock prices from sentiment, no claim of LLM reasoning unless an API is actually connected, and no positioning as a trading system. These match the caveats in the README and the dashboard.

sections.title: Requirements and acceptance criteria
sections.explanation: Functional requirements match the dashboard pages: single and batch input, model choice, probabilities, explainability, error analysis and a separate stock workflow. The success metrics put macro-F1 and stable CV scores first, which matches the evaluation choices elsewhere. The acceptance criteria are operational ('runs from a clean clone', 'pages render without broken imports'). The second one is enforced directly by tests/test_page_imports.py.

data_manifest.toml.overview: A TOML manifest recording every dataset the project uses, for reproducibility: source, licence, sample counts, class distribution, split sizes, seed, local path and label mapping. It is the main artifact for tour step 2. It separates the real training set (PhraseBank AllAgree), the synthetic pipeline-demo headlines and the real MIT-licensed OOD benchmark, so nobody mistakes demo data for evidence.

sections.title: Primary dataset: PhraseBank
sections.explanation: Records Financial PhraseBank AllAgree: 2,264 sentences with 100% annotator agreement, class counts 570/1,391/303, latin-1 encoding, and a stratified 80/10/10 split (1,807/226/226) with seed 42. Keeping the seed and split sizes here lets anyone check that their processed CSVs match. The latin-1 encoding is also what preprocess.load_raw_data uses when it opens the file.

sections.title: Synthetic demo headlines
sections.explanation: Documents the 2,688 template-generated headlines for AAPL, TSLA and AMZN with `synthetic = true`. The comment warns that the `source` column (Reuters, Bloomberg and so on) is assigned at random. The `purpose` field states that this data only exercises the pipeline and is not a generalization benchmark. The section name `cross_validation_dataset` is a leftover from an earlier, less careful framing, and the content now corrects it.

sections.title: Real OOD generalization set
sections.explanation: Defines the real benchmark: zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment, MIT licence, validation split, 2,388 rows, with the fetch command and the Bearish/Bullish/Neutral to negative/positive/neutral mapping. The comments record the results (SVM 0.46, DistilBERT 0.73, FinBERT 0.84 macro-F1). Small discrepancy: this file says FinBERT used 3 epochs and reached 0.88 accuracy, while the README says 4 epochs and 0.87. Be ready to say which run you are quoting.

sections.title: Processed splits and encoding
sections.explanation: Lists the processed CSV paths, the preprocessing steps (regex cleaning, lowercasing, duplicate removal with 5 rows dropped, null check) and the canonical label encoding negative=0, neutral=1, positive=2. That encoding has to match utils.LABEL_MAP. Any model whose native order differs, such as ProsusAI/finbert, must be remapped to it.

scripts/fetch_real_news_dataset.py.overview: A small script that downloads the real, MIT-licensed Twitter Financial News Sentiment validation split from Hugging Face. It maps the dataset's label ids onto the project's scheme and writes data/external/real_financial_news.csv. This produces the OOD benchmark from tour step 2, where the PhraseBank-trained SVM falls to 0.46 macro-F1. The key detail is the label remapping, because the source dataset numbers its classes differently.

sections.title: Docstring: source and mapping
sections.explanation: Explains why this dataset is used: real, human-labelled and licensed, and different from PhraseBank, so it is a true out-of-domain test. It documents the label remapping (0 Bearish -> 0 negative, 1 Bullish -> 2 positive, 2 Neutral -> 1 neutral) and the output columns. A useful interview point: label ids are not universal, and a silent mismatch would make a model look wrong for the wrong reason.

sections.title: Constants and label map
sections.explanation: Paths are resolved from the script's own location (`ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent`), so the script works from any working directory. The dataset name, split and licence are constants. `LABEL_MAP` maps each dataset id to a (project id, project name) tuple, so the numeric and string labels are written from one source of truth. The same mapping appears again as DS_TO_PROJECT in finetune_finbert_news.py.

sections.title: Download, map and write CSV
sections.explanation: `datasets` is imported lazily inside main and exits with a clear install hint if it is missing, so it stays an optional dependency rather than something CI must install. Each example is stripped, empty texts are skipped, the label is mapped, and a `source` column records the dataset and licence for provenance. After writing the CSV it prints the label distribution (useful for spotting imbalance: roughly two-thirds neutral) and the next command to run.

docs/SCHEMA.md.overview: Documents the data contracts shared across the pipeline: the raw PhraseBank format, the integer label encoding, the processed split columns, the names of saved model and result artifacts, and the stock-extension fields. It supports tour step 2 by explaining why every module can assume a `sentence` column and labels 0/1/2. The closing notes make it a guard against schema drift.

sections.title: Raw format and label encoding
sections.explanation: Raw PhraseBank rows are a sentence plus a string label. They are encoded as 0=negative, 1=neutral, 2=positive, which matches utils.LABEL_MAP and the manifest. Writing the encoding down once matters because external models (ProsusAI/finbert uses positive/negative/neutral) and external datasets (Bearish/Bullish/Neutral) all use different orders.

sections.title: Processed split schema
sections.explanation: The processed train/val/test CSVs have exactly two columns: cleaned `sentence` text and an integer `label`. preprocess.create_splits writes them, and train.py, model.py and evaluation read them. This small, stable contract lets the CSVs act as the interface between preprocessing and every downstream consumer.

sections.title: Model and result artifacts
sections.explanation: Lists the seven baseline joblib files and the result JSONs (evaluation, CV, cross-dataset, SHAP). The naming convention `baseline_<name>.joblib` is what train.py writes and what the predictor discovers. The results/*.json files are what the dashboard reads instead of recomputing metrics.

sections.title: Stock fields and schema rules
sections.explanation: Defines the fields of the experimental stock extension: ticker, date, headline, sentiment and next-day direction. The notes give practical rules: keep the schema stable, do not rename `sentence` to `text` in only some scripts, and update every loader when fields change. Interestingly, the real-news CSV uses `headline` rather than `sentence`, so the code that reads it has to handle that difference.

src/preprocess.py.overview: The data-preparation module for tour step 3. It reads Financial PhraseBank at a chosen annotator-agreement level, removes duplicate and empty rows, cleans the text, encodes labels as integers using the shared LABEL_MAP, and writes stratified train/val/test CSVs with a fixed seed. Training, evaluation and SHAP all read those files, so this module decides what counts as held-out data for the whole project.

sections.title: Imports and logger
sections.explanation: Imports scikit-learn's train_test_split and three helpers from utils: LABEL_MAP, get_project_root and setup_logging. Taking the label map from utils, rather than redefining it here, ensures preprocessing and inference agree on what 0, 1 and 2 mean. Note the bare `from utils import`: src/ is expected to be on the import path, which is why other scripts insert it into sys.path.

sections.title: Loading raw PhraseBank
sections.explanation: Builds the path from the agreement level (50Agree up to AllAgree), so changing the label-quality trade-off is a single argument. Files are read as latin-1 because the original release is not UTF-8. Each line is split with `rsplit('@', 1)`, splitting only on the last '@', so a sentence that itself contains '@' stays intact. Lines without an '@' are silently skipped.

sections.title: Loading processed splits
sections.explanation: A thin loader for data/processed/{split}.csv that every training and evaluation function uses, so they all read the same frozen splits. It raises FileNotFoundError when the file is missing. The message still says 'Run EDA notebook first', although the real producer is `python src/preprocess.py`, a small stale detail.

sections.title: Text cleaning rules
sections.explanation: Lowercases the text, collapses whitespace and removes every character except word characters, whitespace and `. , % $ - +`. Those symbols are kept on purpose because numbers, percentages and signs carry financial meaning ('up 5%', '-3.2'). Stopwords are not removed. The interview guide lists that as a limitation, since SHAP later shows the model relying on words like 'is' and 'the'.

sections.title: De-duplication and encoding
sections.explanation: Works on a copy, drops duplicate sentences and empty or null rows, optionally cleans, and maps string labels to integers only when the column is still `object` dtype, so the function is safe to call twice. Removing duplicates before splitting is the main leakage guard: the same sentence cannot end up in both train and test. One subtle gotcha: de-duplication runs before cleaning, so two sentences that differ only in case or punctuation become identical after cleaning and can both survive.

sections.title: Stratified two-stage split
sections.explanation: Splits in two stages: 80% train vs 20% temp, then temp into 50/50 val and test. Both stages use `stratify=` and `random_state=42`. Stratification keeps the roughly 61/25/14 class mix in every split, which matters because negatives are only about 14% and a random split could leave the small test set short of them. The fixed seed makes the 1,807/226/226 split reproducible and matches the manifest.

sections.title: Saving and pipeline entry
sections.explanation: save_processed_data writes the three CSVs and logs their sizes. prepare_data chains load -> preprocess -> split -> save and logs the row count after preprocessing, which shows how many duplicates were removed. Running the module directly regenerates the splits, and every downstream step depends on them.

src/utils.py.overview: The shared foundation module with the highest fan-in in the project. It defines the canonical label mapping, the lists of supported model names, path helpers anchored to the project root, a logging factory that avoids duplicate handlers, and descriptive model metadata that is joined with real evaluation results. Tour step 3 points to it as the reason label encoding stays consistent across preprocessing, training, inference and the UI.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Only the standard library is used (json, logging, sys, pathlib, typing). That is deliberate: a module everyone imports should be cheap and must not pull in torch or scikit-learn, so lightweight consumers such as CI tests and the API can import it freely.

sections.title: Label maps and model lists
sections.explanation: `LABEL_MAP = {negative: 0, neutral: 1, positive: 2}` and its inverse are the single source of truth for label encoding. Putting them in one module is what makes remapping external orders (FinBERT, the Twitter dataset) a clear, testable step instead of a hidden bug. BASELINE_CLASSIFIERS and TRANSFORMER_MODELS list the supported names. TRANSFORMER_MODELS does not include 'deberta', although model.py supports it.

sections.title: Path helpers
sections.explanation: get_project_root returns the parent of src/ using `__file__`, so paths work whatever the current directory is (scripts, tests, Streamlit or Docker). get_model_dir and get_results_dir create their directories when missing, so writers never fail on a fresh clone. get_data_dir does not create anything, which suits a read-oriented helper.

sections.title: Logging factory
sections.explanation: setup_logging returns a named logger with a stdout handler and a consistent format. The `if not logger.handlers` check stops duplicate handlers being added when a module is imported or reloaded more than once, which is common under Streamlit reruns and pytest. Without it every log line would be printed several times.

sections.title: Descriptive model metadata
sections.explanation: A dict of display names, model types, speed tiers and feature bullet points for each model key. The comment makes a point of design: no metrics are hardcoded here, so the UI cannot show numbers that disagree with the evaluation. Note an inconsistency: the 'finbert' entry says it was fine-tuned on Financial PhraseBank, but the shipped fine-tuned FinBERT was trained on the news dataset (scripts/finetune_finbert_news.py).

sections.title: Joining metadata with results
sections.explanation: get_model_info starts from the metadata with 'N/A' metrics, then fills in accuracy and F1 from results/evaluation_results.json if a matching entry exists. Corrupt JSON or missing keys are caught, so the UI shows N/A instead of crashing. This puts the 'results as artifacts' principle into practice: displayed numbers are read from what evaluation produced. get_all_model_info simply maps the function over a list of models.

src/train.py.overview: The classical-ML training module for tour step 4. It builds TF-IDF + classifier scikit-learn Pipelines for six models, trains a soft-voting ensemble with a calibrated SVM, runs 5-fold stratified cross-validation and GridSearchCV tuning scored on macro-F1, and saves joblib artifacts and JSON results. It also delegates transformer training to model.py and has a CLI with modes such as baselines, cv and tune. The strong baselines built here are the bar that FinBERT has to beat.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports everything for classical text classification: TfidfVectorizer, six classifier families, CalibratedClassifierCV, VotingClassifier, Pipeline, and the CV and tuning tools (StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, GridSearchCV, make_scorer). Data comes only through preprocess.load_processed_data, so training always uses the frozen splits from step 3.

sections.title: TF-IDF pipeline factory
sections.explanation: One factory builds every baseline as Pipeline([tfidf, classifier]). The shared TF-IDF settings are unigrams+bigrams, 10k features, min_df=2 and max_df=0.95; bigrams capture phrases like 'fell sharply'. LogReg, SVM and RF use `class_weight='balanced'` to counter the neutral majority, and every model has random_state=42. Because the vectorizer is inside the pipeline, it is refit on each CV training fold (no leakage), and the whole object is saved as one artifact.

sections.title: Train and compare baselines
sections.explanation: train_baseline fits on train, scores on val (accuracy, macro and weighted F1, classification report) and saves `baseline_<name>.joblib`. train_all_baselines loops over six models and picks the best by val macro-F1. These are single-split numbers on 226 rows, which is why the project relies on CV rather than this comparison to choose a model.

sections.title: Soft-voting ensemble
sections.explanation: Combines LogReg, a calibrated SVM and a Random Forest with `voting='soft'`, averaging class probabilities. LinearSVC has no predict_proba, so it is wrapped in CalibratedClassifierCV(cv=3), which fits a calibration mapping on internal folds. Unlike the baselines, the vectorizer is fitted separately and saved as a dict `{tfidf, ensemble}`. That is why predict.py needs a separate branch to transform the text before calling the ensemble.

sections.title: Loading and transformer delegate
sections.explanation: load_model is a simple joblib loader keyed by artifact name. train_transformer is a thin wrapper that imports model.train_transformer only when called. The lazy import keeps torch and transformers out of the import path for anyone using only the classical baselines, which keeps light environments such as CI fast.

sections.title: Train everything
sections.explanation: Trains three baselines plus FinBERT and DistilBERT on PhraseBank and logs a combined comparison. Transformer failures are caught and logged so that one heavy model does not stop the run. Note that this 'all' mode trains transformers on PhraseBank. The news-fine-tuned models reported in the README come from scripts/finetune_finbert_news.py instead.

sections.title: Stratified k-fold CV
sections.explanation: Combines train+val (2,033 rows) and runs cross_validate with StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle, seed 42), scoring accuracy, macro-F1 and weighted F1 in parallel. It records mean, std and per-fold scores in results/cv_results.json. The test split is never touched, so it stays a clean final check. This is where the 0.838 +/- 0.016 SVM figure comes from, and why the project reports CV scores and not only one noisy 226-row test score.

sections.title: GridSearchCV tuning
sections.explanation: Tunes the SVM (C in {0.1..5} x max_iter in {1000, 2000} = 10 combinations) and Gradient Boosting (2x3x3 = 18) with 5-fold stratified CV and a macro-F1 scorer, using `refit=True`. Gotcha: the best estimators, refit on train+val, overwrite baseline_svm.joblib and baseline_gradient_boosting.joblib, so the saved artifacts depend on whether tuning ran last. numpy integer and float values in best_params are converted before json.dump, which would otherwise fail on them.

sections.title: CLI dispatch
sections.explanation: argparse maps `--model` to a mode: all, baselines (which also trains the ensemble), ensemble, cv, tune, a transformer name or a single baseline. Transformer runs pass through the epochs, batch-size and lr flags. This is the entry point that scripts/retrain.py and the README commands use.

src/model.py.overview: The transformer fine-tuning engine for tour step 5. FinancialSentimentModel wraps a Hugging Face AutoModelForSequenceClassification with a tokenizing Dataset, an AdamW + linear-warmup loop, optional class-weighted cross-entropy, mixed precision on CUDA (disabled for DeBERTa), gradient clipping, best-checkpoint restore by validation macro-F1 with optional early stopping, plus evaluate, predict and save/load helpers. scripts/finetune_finbert_news.py reuses it to fine-tune on news, and predict.py loads its saved models.

sections.title: Imports and backbone registry
sections.explanation: MODELS maps short names to Hub checkpoints: FinBERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, BERT and DeBERTa-v3 (which needs sentencepiece). The Auto* classes let the same wrapper fine-tune any of these architectures without code changes. get_linear_schedule_with_warmup provides the standard BERT learning-rate schedule.

sections.title: Tokenizing Dataset
sections.explanation: A PyTorch Dataset that tokenizes each text when it is requested, with truncation and fixed padding to max_length=128, and returns input_ids, attention_mask and a long label tensor. 128 tokens comfortably covers short sentences and headlines while keeping memory low. Fixed-length padding is simple but less efficient than dynamic padding per batch, an optimisation you could mention.

sections.title: Model initialisation
sections.explanation: Validates the model name, picks CUDA when available, and loads the tokenizer and a classification model with num_labels=3. `ignore_mismatched_sizes=True` lets checkpoints with a different head size load with a fresh head. For ProsusAI/finbert the head is already 3-way, so its weights are kept and fine-tuning simply re-learns them for the project's label order. The code does not set id2label or label2id, so the saved config.json keeps the base checkpoint's label names. That is the label-name issue the guard test and the upload script now check.

sections.title: Optimizer, loss and AMP setup
sections.explanation: Uses AdamW with a linear schedule and 10% warmup. Warmup avoids large early updates that would damage pre-trained weights. Optional class weights go into CrossEntropyLoss to raise minority-class recall, which targets macro-F1. AMP (fp16 autocast with a GradScaler) is enabled only on CUDA and explicitly not for the DeBERTa family, the fix for the mixed-precision crash described in the interview guide.

sections.title: Training loop and checkpointing
sections.explanation: Each step runs the forward pass under autocast, casts logits to float32 before the loss (needed when the model outputs fp16 but the class weights are fp32), then scales the loss, runs backward, unscales and clips gradients to norm 1.0 before stepping. Unscaling before clipping matters, otherwise the clip threshold would apply to scaled gradients. After every epoch it evaluates and keeps a CPU copy of the best state by val macro-F1, with optional patience-based early stopping. At the end it restores the best weights, so the saved model is the best epoch, not the last.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.explanation: Runs in eval mode under no_grad, collects argmax predictions and returns loss, accuracy, macro and weighted F1, and the raw y_true/y_pred arrays for reports. The reported loss comes from the model's built-in, unweighted loss (`labels=` passed to forward), so validation loss is not directly comparable to a class-weighted training loss.

sections.title: Batch and single prediction
sections.explanation: predict reuses the DataLoader with dummy labels, applies softmax and returns predictions and probabilities. predict_single turns these into the project's standard {prediction, label, confidence, probabilities} dict using LABEL_MAP_INV, the same shape the baselines return, which is what lets SentimentPredictor treat all models alike.

sections.title: Save and load
sections.explanation: save writes the model and tokenizer to models/{name}_finetuned/ with save_pretrained, which is the folder predict.py looks for. load is a classmethod that builds an instance without calling __init__ (so no base checkpoint is downloaded) and accepts either a local path or a Hub repo id. It keeps the identifier as a string so ids like 'user/finbert-financial' are not mangled by Windows path handling, which supports the Hub fallback used in deployment.

sections.title: PhraseBank training entry
sections.explanation: train_transformer loads the PhraseBank splits, trains, evaluates on val, logs a classification report and saves. It does not pass class weights or early stopping, so the PhraseBank path uses the plain recipe. The news fine-tuning script enables those options. Running the module directly trains FinBERT for 3 epochs.

src/finbert_pretrained.py.overview: Runs the off-the-shelf ProsusAI/finbert checkpoint zero-shot, with no training. Its main job is to translate FinBERT's native label order (0=positive, 1=negative, 2=neutral) into the project's scheme (0=negative, 1=neutral, 2=positive) for both the predicted label and the probability vector. Tour step 5 uses it as the zero-shot side of the zero-shot vs fine-tuned comparison. A module-level singleton keeps the roughly 440 MB model from being loaded more than once.

sections.title: Native label order and revision
sections.explanation: LABEL_MAP here is FinBERT's own order, `{0: positive, 1: negative, 2: neutral}`, which differs from the project's map. Defining it on the class keeps the translation in one visible place. MODEL_REVISION is passed to from_pretrained for supply-chain-safe loads, but its value is 'main', a moving branch rather than a commit hash. The interview guide lists that as a limitation: pin a SHA for truly reproducible loads.

sections.title: Model loading
sections.explanation: Picks CUDA when available, loads the tokenizer and model at the pinned revision, moves the model to the device and calls `eval()` straight away. Inference-only use means dropout is off from the start, so predictions are deterministic.

sections.title: Batched predict with remapping
sections.explanation: Accepts a single string or a list, then processes batches of 8 to limit memory, with padding and truncation at 512 tokens. For each output it maps the argmax through FinBERT's label map, converts the name to the project id, and explicitly rebuilds the probability dict (negative=prob[1], neutral=prob[2], positive=prob[0]). Without that reordering, positive and negative probabilities would be silently swapped. This is the label-order bug interviewers ask about. The returned text is truncated to 100 characters for display.

sections.title: Cached singleton accessors
sections.explanation: get_finbert lazily creates one global PretrainedFinBERT, so repeated calls (several dashboard pages, benchmarks) share one loaded model. predict_with_finbert returns a single dict for string input and a list for list input, which mirrors the input type for convenience.

sections.title: Manual smoke test
sections.explanation: Running the module directly prints predictions for three handwritten sentences (positive, negative, neutral). It is a quick manual check that the label remapping looks right, not an automated test.

scripts/finetune_finbert_news.py.overview: The experiment that tests whether the out-of-domain gap comes from domain mismatch. It fine-tunes a transformer (DistilBERT by default, FinBERT for the headline result) on the train split of the Twitter financial news dataset and evaluates on its full validation split, the same rows on which the PhraseBank SVM scored 0.46. It reuses FinancialSentimentModel from src/model.py and turns on class weights and early stopping through flags. It saves models/{name}_finetuned/ for the dashboard and API to pick up. This is the 0.84 macro-F1 result in tour steps 5 and 8.

sections.title: Purpose and label mapping
sections.explanation: The docstring frames the experiment honestly: this is in-domain training for the news distribution, so it shows that domain-matched data closes the gap. It does not show that FinBERT generalizes zero-shot. src/ is added to sys.path so that `model` and `utils` import as in the rest of the codebase. DS_TO_PROJECT repeats the Bearish/Bullish/Neutral remapping from the fetch script.

sections.title: Loading news splits
sections.explanation: Loads a split straight from Hugging Face and optionally caps it with `select(range(max_n))`. That keeps the first N rows, not a shuffled or stratified sample, which is fine for a CPU smoke run but could change the class mix. Unlike the fetch script, it does not drop empty texts.

sections.title: CLI, device and class weights
sections.explanation: Flags control the backbone, epochs, batch size, lr, a training cap, the size of the validation subset used for monitoring, class weights, early stopping and patience. Heavy imports (torch, model) happen after argument parsing, so `--help` stays fast. With `--class-weights` it computes inverse-frequency weights `N / (3 * count_c)`, guarding against zero counts, so the rarer negative and positive classes count more in the loss. That directly targets macro-F1 against neutral dominance.

sections.title: Train, evaluate, save
sections.explanation: Trains with per-epoch monitoring on only the first `--val-monitor` (500) validation rows, then evaluates on the full validation split and saves. The best epoch is chosen on rows that are also part of the final reported set, which is the small optimistic selection bias the README admits. The clean fix is a separate dev split carved out of train.

sections.title: Writing results
sections.explanation: Writes the metrics to results/finetune_results.json and to a per-model file, so parallel DistilBERT and FinBERT runs do not overwrite each other. The dataset string records that this is an in-domain train->val evaluation. The final printout compares the result directly with the ~0.46 PhraseBank baseline, which is the story this script exists to tell.

tests/test_model_artifacts.py.overview: A small guard test on the committed fine-tuned FinBERT checkpoint. It checks that the `id2label`/`label2id` entries in `models/finbert_finetuned/config.json` match the project's own label mapping in `utils.LABEL_MAP_INV`. This is the label-order safety net described in tour step 5: the app decodes predictions itself, but anyone who loads the checkpoint with a Hugging Face `pipeline()` relies on the config's names.

sections.title: Path setup and imports
sections.explanation: Adds `src/` to `sys.path` so the test can import `LABEL_MAP_INV` from `utils` without the project being an installed package. The `# noqa: E402` comment tells Ruff to allow an import that comes after code. Importing the mapping from the single shared module (rather than hard-coding labels) means the test follows any change to the project's label scheme.

sections.title: Config label consistency test
sections.explanation: Reads the committed `config.json` and makes two checks. First, `id2label` (JSON keys are strings, so they are cast to `int`) must equal `LABEL_MAP_INV`. Second, `label2id` must be its exact inverse. The docstring gives the reason: the classification head was trained on the project's ids (0=negative, 1=neutral, 2=positive), and if the config used a different order, a `pipeline()` user would silently get wrong label names. Good interview point: label-order mismatches cause no error, so you guard them with a cheap test on the artifact itself.

src/predict.py.overview: Defines `SentimentPredictor`, the single interface the dashboard and the FastAPI service use for every model type: joblib TF-IDF baselines, the voting ensemble, off-the-shelf FinBERT and fine-tuned transformers. Every model returns the same dict shape (label, integer prediction, confidence, per-class probabilities). It also handles deployment: when local transformer weights are missing or are only Git LFS pointer files, it loads them from a Hugging Face Hub repo named by an environment variable. This is the architectural hinge described in tour step 6.

sections.title: Imports and logger
sections.explanation: Imports only light dependencies at module level (joblib, numpy, pandas) plus the shared `LABEL_MAP_INV` and path helpers from `utils`. Heavy libraries such as torch/transformers are imported lazily inside `_load_model`, so a process serving only TF-IDF baselines never pays the transformer import cost. This matters for CI and for small containers.

sections.title: Hub repo and LFS pointer helpers
sections.explanation: `_finetuned_hf_repo` reads `FINSIGHT_<MODEL>_REPO` from the environment, which lets a deployment point at a Hub repo without code changes. `_has_usable_local_weights` handles a real deployment problem: hosts that do not pull Git LFS (for example Streamlit Community Cloud) check out `model.safetensors` as a ~130-byte text pointer. The function treats a weights file as real only if it is larger than 1 MB, so a pointer counts as 'no weights' and triggers the Hub fallback instead of a confusing load error.

sections.title: Constructor and model-type routing
sections.explanation: The constructor takes a model-type string and derives two flags: `is_pretrained_finbert` and `is_transformer` (anything not prefixed `baseline_` and not the pre-trained FinBERT). These flags drive both loading and prediction dispatch. Loading happens eagerly in `__init__`, so a bad model name fails at construction time rather than on the first request. That is why the API and UI cache predictor instances.

sections.title: Loading each model family
sections.explanation: Three branches. Pre-trained FinBERT comes from `finbert_pretrained.get_finbert()`. Fine-tuned transformers load from `models/<type>_finetuned` when usable weights exist, otherwise from the Hub repo; if neither exists, the error message tells the user how to fix it (train, or set the env var). Baselines load from `<type>.joblib`. The ensemble is stored as a dict `{tfidf, ensemble}` rather than a Pipeline, so it is detected and flagged with `is_ensemble`.

sections.title: Public predict and dispatch
sections.explanation: `predict` accepts either a string or a list. It always wraps the input into a list, runs one batch path, and unwraps the result for single inputs. This keeps a single code path while giving callers a convenient API. `_predict_batch` routes on the flags set in the constructor, which is a simple strategy pattern without a class hierarchy.

sections.title: Baseline prediction and probabilities
sections.explanation: Normalises scikit-learn outputs into the shared result dict. It uses `predict_proba` when the pipeline has it (the SVM is calibrated in training, so it usually does). Otherwise it falls back to a numerically stable softmax over `decision_function` scores (subtracting the row max before `exp`). Those pseudo-probabilities are not calibrated, so they should be read as relative scores. Long texts are truncated to 100 characters in the echoed `text` field to keep responses small.

sections.title: Ensemble and transformer prediction
sections.explanation: The ensemble path applies the stored TF-IDF vectorizer and then the soft-voting classifier, whose `predict_proba` averages member probabilities. The transformer path expects `FinancialSentimentModel.predict` to return `(predictions, probabilities)`. Both produce the same keys as the baseline path, so downstream code (API schemas, dashboard widgets) does not need to know which model ran. Labels are always decoded with `LABEL_MAP_INV`, not the checkpoint config.

sections.title: File prediction helper
sections.explanation: Batch-scores a CSV (from a named text column) or a TXT file (one non-empty line per text) and appends `predicted_label`, `predicted_class` and `confidence` columns to a DataFrame. Unsupported extensions raise a clear `ValueError`. It reuses `_predict_batch`, so file scoring behaves exactly like API scoring.

sections.title: Convenience functions and model discovery
sections.explanation: `predict_single`/`predict_batch` are one-off wrappers that build a new predictor on every call, which is fine for scripts but not for serving. `get_available_models` builds the model selector list: baselines whose joblib exists, pre-trained FinBERT always (it downloads on demand), and fine-tuned transformers only when real local weights exist or a Hub repo is configured. DistilBERT is left out on purpose, as the comment says, so FinBERT stays the single production fine-tuned model.

sections.title: Command-line interface
sections.explanation: A small argparse CLI with four modes: `--list-models`, a single `--text`, a `--file` batch with optional `--output` CSV, and an interactive REPL by default. The REPL builds the predictor once and reuses it across inputs, which avoids reloading the model per line.

scripts/upload_finetuned_to_hf.py.overview: A one-off publishing script that uploads a locally fine-tuned transformer folder to the Hugging Face Hub. The ~417 MB FinBERT weights exceed GitHub's 100 MB file limit, so the deployed app fetches them from the Hub through `predict.py`'s `FINSIGHT_<MODEL>_REPO` fallback (tour step 6). Before uploading it validates the label mapping, so the published checkpoint cannot mislead `pipeline()` users.

sections.title: Docstring: rationale and usage
sections.explanation: Records why the script exists (the weights are too large for git) and the full workflow: create a write-scoped token, log in, run the upload, then set `FINSIGHT_FINBERT_REPO` as a deployment secret. Writing the operational steps next to the code helps when you need to explain how large artifacts reach a cloud deployment.

sections.title: Imports and path setup
sections.explanation: Adds `src/` to the path so the script reuses `LABEL_MAP_INV` and `get_model_dir` from `utils`. The upload therefore resolves the same `models/` directory and label scheme as training and serving.

sections.title: Arguments and pre-upload validation
sections.explanation: Parses `--model`, a required `--repo`, `--private` and an optional `--token`. It then fails fast in two cases: the local folder is missing, or `config.json`'s `id2label` does not match the project labels. This mirrors the check in `tests/test_model_artifacts.py`, applied at publish time so a mislabeled checkpoint never reaches the Hub. A missing README model card only gives a warning, because it affects documentation rather than correctness.

sections.title: Repo creation and folder upload
sections.explanation: Imports `huggingface_hub` lazily so the rest of the project does not depend on it, and gives a clear install hint if it is missing. `create_repo(..., exist_ok=True)` makes reruns idempotent, and `upload_folder` pushes config, tokenizer and weights in one commit. The final message prints the exact secret name to set, which links the upload back to the runtime fallback in `predict.py`.

.gitattributes.overview: Git attributes that route large binary files through Git LFS. In this project it covers the fine-tuned FinBERT `.safetensors` weights and a raw data folder. It explains the deployment problem `predict.py` works around (tour step 6): hosts that do not pull LFS check out small pointer files instead of real weights.

sections.title: LFS tracking rules
sections.explanation: Each line matches a path pattern and sets `filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text`. Git stores a small text pointer in the repository and keeps the real bytes in LFS storage, and `-text` stops line-ending conversion on binary data. Line 1 tracks a dataset folder whose name contains a space (written as `[[:space:]]`). Line 2 tracks `models/finbert_finetuned/*.safetensors`. If a clone skips `git lfs pull`, that file is a ~130-byte pointer, which is why `_has_usable_local_weights` checks for a size above 1 MB before trusting local weights.

src/evaluate.py.overview: The in-domain evaluation module. It scores saved baselines and fine-tuned transformers on a processed split (default `test`) and computes accuracy plus macro and weighted F1, precision and recall. It also prints per-class reports, plots confusion matrices, compares all available models, runs error analysis on misclassifications, and saves JSON results. It is the point-estimate side of tour step 7; `stats.py` and `bootstrap_ci.py` add the uncertainty intervals.

sections.title: Imports and logger
sections.explanation: Pulls in the scikit-learn metric functions and the confusion-matrix display, `load_processed_data` (so evaluation reads exactly the splits written by preprocessing), and the shared label mapping and path helpers from `utils`.

sections.title: Evaluating baselines and transformers
sections.explanation: `evaluate_baseline` loads `baseline_<name>.joblib` and predicts on the split's `sentence` column. The voting ensemble is saved as a `{tfidf, ensemble}` dict rather than a Pipeline, so it is special-cased. `evaluate_transformer` imports the transformer wrapper lazily, delegates to `model.evaluate`, and adds macro and weighted precision/recall so both model families report the same metric set. Both raise `FileNotFoundError` with a 'train first' hint when the artifact is missing.

sections.title: Shared metric computation
sections.explanation: One function returns every metric plus the raw `y_true`/`y_pred` arrays, so later steps (confusion matrices, error analysis, JSON export) can reuse the predictions without rerunning the model. Macro-F1 is reported next to accuracy because the labels are imbalanced (mostly neutral): macro-F1 weights every class equally, so a model that ignores the minority classes cannot hide behind a high accuracy.

sections.title: Report printing and confusion matrix
sections.explanation: `print_evaluation_report` prints headline metrics and scikit-learn's per-class `classification_report`, with class names ordered by label id via `LABEL_MAP_INV`. `plot_confusion_matrix` draws a matplotlib heatmap and can save it at 150 dpi. Building `target_names` from the sorted mapping keeps axis labels aligned with the integer encoding.

sections.title: Multi-model comparison
sections.explanation: Discovers every baseline joblib and transformer folder that exists, evaluates each, and prints a table sorted by macro-F1 that names the best model. Each model is wrapped in try/except so one broken artifact does not stop the whole comparison; the error is logged instead. Ranking by macro-F1 rather than accuracy matches the project's primary metric.

sections.title: Error analysis
sections.explanation: Finds misclassified rows, counts each off-diagonal confusion pattern (for example `neutral_as_positive`), prints sample texts, and prints simple insights depending on which patterns appear. The returned dict holds error rate, pattern counts and samples. This supports the qualitative interview answer: most errors involve the neutral class, either neutral read as polar or subtle polar sentences read as neutral.

sections.title: Saving results and CLI
sections.explanation: `save_results` copies each metrics dict and converts numpy arrays to lists so it serialises to `results/evaluation_results.json`. The CLI supports a single model (with optional `--plot` or `--errors`) or a comparison of all models (with optional `--save` and `--plot`).

src/stats.py.overview: The single shared implementation of macro-F1 and percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals. Baselines, FinBERT and the LLM benchmark all get their intervals from `bootstrap_macro_f1`, so the comparisons in tour steps 7, 8 and 10 are computed the same way. It also provides `pairs_from_confusion`, which rebuilds evaluation rows from a saved confusion matrix.

sections.title: Module purpose and label ids
sections.explanation: The docstring states the design decision: one implementation behind every reported interval, so intervals stay comparable across model families. `LABEL_IDS = [0, 1, 2]` fixes the classes that macro-F1 averages over, independent of which labels happen to appear in a given sample or prediction set.

sections.title: Macro-F1 with fixed labels
sections.explanation: Wraps scikit-learn's `f1_score` with `average='macro'`, `labels=LABEL_IDS` and `zero_division=0`. Passing explicit labels has two effects. A prediction outside the classes (such as `-1` for an invalid LLM answer) counts as wrong rather than adding a fourth class. A bootstrap resample that misses a class still averages over all three, scoring that class as 0 instead of raising a warning or changing the denominator.

sections.title: Percentile bootstrap
sections.explanation: Validates that the inputs are non-empty and the same length. It then resamples row indices with replacement `n_boot` times (default 2,000), recomputes macro-F1 on each resample, and takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95% interval. The optional `rng` lets a caller share one random stream across several intervals, which keeps a whole report reproducible from a single seed. `tail` is rounded to avoid floating-point values like 2.500000000000002. The point estimate is always macro-F1 on the full, unresampled data.

sections.title: Rebuilding pairs from a confusion matrix
sections.explanation: Turns a confusion matrix (rows = true, columns = predicted) back into parallel `y_true`/`y_pred` arrays by repeating each `(t, p)` pair `count` times. Macro-F1 depends only on these pairs, not on row order or text, so bootstrapping the rebuilt pairs is equivalent to bootstrapping the original rows. This lets the project compute real-news CIs from saved JSON results without rerunning the models.

scripts/bootstrap_ci.py.overview: Computes 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for macro-F1 and writes `results/bootstrap_ci.json`. It re-scores every saved baseline on the 226-row PhraseBank test split, and it rebuilds the 2,388-row real-news results for SVM and FinBERT from their saved confusion matrices. The Generalization dashboard page reads this file to draw its interval charts (tour steps 7 and 8).

sections.title: Docstring: why intervals
sections.explanation: Explains the motivation: on a 226-row test set a single score can move a lot with a different sample, so a point estimate alone overstates precision. It also documents the shortcut for real news, where resampling the (true, predicted) pairs from a confusion matrix is equivalent to resampling the rows. This is a good answer to 'what does a CI tell you on n=226?'.

sections.title: Imports and constants
sections.explanation: Reuses `load_processed_data` (same test split as evaluation), `bootstrap_macro_f1`/`pairs_from_confusion` from the shared stats module, and the path helpers. `N_BOOT=2000` and `SEED=42` are fixed constants so the published intervals can be reproduced exactly. `BASELINES` lists every classical model including the ensemble.

sections.title: Helpers
sections.explanation: `_ci` fixes the resample count and passes through a shared generator. `_predict` handles the ensemble's dict format (`tfidf` then `ensemble`), using the same convention as `evaluate.py` and `predict.py`.

sections.title: Main: score, resample, write
sections.explanation: Creates one `default_rng(SEED)` and passes it to every interval, so the whole file comes from one reproducible random stream. Missing artifacts are skipped instead of failing, so the script works with whatever has been trained. It writes the JSON with metadata (`n_boot`, `seed`, `confidence`) next to the results and prints a readable table of each score and its interval.

scripts/compare_ood.py.overview: Combines the per-model out-of-domain results into one comparison artifact, `results/model_comparison_ood.json`. The dashboard and README read this file. It collects `generalization_<model>.json` files (held-out real-news evaluation) and, for models that have no such file yet, `finetune_results_*.json` files labeled as training-time numbers. This is the summary input for the central OOD finding in tour step 8.

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: Documents the prerequisite: run `integrate_news.py --action generalization` per model first, then this script. Only `get_results_dir` is imported, so the script does no model work; it only reshapes saved results.

sections.title: Collecting generalization results
sections.explanation: Iterates over `generalization_*.json` in sorted order, skipping the aggregate `generalization_results.json`. A `seen` set removes duplicate model names. Dataset-level fields (majority-class accuracy, dataset name, sample count) are carried forward from whichever files contain them. Each entry is tagged `source: generalization_eval` so readers know it comes from a held-out evaluation.

sections.title: Fallback to fine-tune results
sections.explanation: Adds fine-tune results only for models with no generalization file. These entries are tagged `finetune_train_eval` and carry a note saying they are training-time numbers. Labeling the source of each metric keeps the comparison honest, because a training-time score should not be presented as a held-out OOD result.

sections.title: Sorting, writing and reporting
sections.explanation: Exits with a message if nothing was found. Otherwise it sorts models by ascending macro-F1 (so the chart reads from weakest to strongest), writes the compact JSON with the majority-class baseline included for context, and prints a summary line per model.

app/views/7_Sentiment_Trends.py.overview: The Streamlit 'Generalization' page. It reports how models trained on PhraseBank hold up on real financial news, using precomputed results: headline KPIs, macro-F1 with bootstrap intervals against a majority-class reference, FinBERT's confusion matrix, an LLM-vs-FinBERT cost and latency comparison, and then a clearly labeled synthetic pipeline demo, SHAP importances and CV intervals. It is the dashboard view of the OOD finding in tour step 8. It never computes headline metrics live; it only reads JSON files from `results/`.

sections.title: Imports and shared UI helpers
sections.explanation: Adds `src/` and `app/` to `sys.path` and imports the design-system helpers from `shared` (KPI strip, exhibit headers, interval charts, source notes, empty and status states). Using shared components keeps styling and wording consistent across all dashboard pages.

sections.title: Page setup and KPI strip
sections.explanation: `active_model()` returns the sidebar-selected model and predictor, and the page stops if none loads. It loads three result files: `generalization_results.json`, `model_comparison_ood.json` and the `real_news` part of `bootstrap_ci.json`. The KPIs put SVM real-news accuracy next to the always-neutral accuracy, which shows that its ~0.67 accuracy barely beats the majority baseline, and they place the SVM's macro-F1 beside the in-domain CV number and fine-tuned FinBERT's score.

sections.title: Macro-F1 intervals on real news
sections.explanation: Builds interval-chart rows for SVM (out-of-domain) and fine-tuned FinBERT (in-domain) from the bootstrap file. The reference line is the macro-F1 of always predicting neutral: precision equals the majority share `maj`, recall is 1, so neutral F1 = 2·maj/(1+maj); the other two classes score 0, and the result is divided by 3. The source note discloses that FinBERT chose its best epoch on 500 of these rows, so its score is slightly optimistic. Stating this limitation directly is a good point to mention in an interview.

sections.title: FinBERT confusion matrix heatmap
sections.explanation: If `generalization_finbert.json` contains a confusion matrix, it is drawn as a Plotly heatmap with direction glyphs on the axis labels, count annotations, and a reversed y-axis so the diagonal runs top-left to bottom-right. The subtitle states the finding: most remaining errors are neutral headlines predicted as polar.

sections.title: LLM vs FinBERT benchmark
sections.explanation: Reads `llm_benchmark.json`. If there are no runs, it shows an empty state explaining that the benchmark needs an API key and suggests `--dry-run` for a free preview. Otherwise it puts the LLM zero-shot and few-shot intervals on the same chart as FinBERT and SVM, then adds a table of macro-F1, interval, cost per 1k headlines, p50/p95 latency and invalid-answer count. It warns when the LLM ran on a stratified subsample, because a smaller n gives wider intervals.

sections.title: Synthetic pipeline demo and correlations
sections.explanation: Imports `integrate_news` optionally and stops with a banner if it is missing. The section header says the data is template-generated and 'not evidence about markets', which keeps synthetic results separate from real metrics. Correlation p-values come from the t-statistic t = r·sqrt((n−2)/(1−r²)) with n−2 degrees of freedom, and the caption reports how many coefficients reach p < 0.05.

sections.title: Interactive sentiment and price chart
sections.explanation: On button click it maps the selected baseline to a short model key (SVM by default for non-baselines), calls `get_sentiment_trends`, and draws a two-row subplot: close price on top and daily mean sentiment bars below, colored by sign. It adds four summary metrics. `FileNotFoundError` and other errors are shown with `st.error` so a missing artifact does not crash the page.

sections.title: SHAP importance display
sections.explanation: Lists the `results/shap_*.json` files written by `shap_explain.py` and, for each model, shows a horizontal bar chart of the top 15 mean-|SHAP| features plus three per-class tables of signed values (top 5 each). If no files exist, it shows the exact command to generate them. This page only displays precomputed explanations and never runs SHAP live.

sections.title: Cross-validation intervals
sections.explanation: Reads `cv_results.json`, ranks models by mean 5-fold macro-F1, highlights the best, and draws mean ± 1 standard deviation bands. The subtitle points out that SVM and Gradient Boosting overlap, meaning the data cannot reliably tell them apart. That supports reporting CV next to a single 226-row test score.

docs/MODEL_CARD.md.overview: The project's model card, modeled on Mitchell et al. (2019). It lists every shipped model with its training data and intended use, reports in-domain and real-news OOD metrics, documents provenance, limitations and ethical considerations, and gives the reproduction commands. It is the written record of the central OOD finding in tour step 8: SVM macro-F1 drops from about 0.90 in-domain to 0.46 on real news, and fine-tuned FinBERT reaches 0.84.

sections.title: Models at a glance
sections.explanation: A table of each model family (TF-IDF baselines, zero-shot ProsusAI/finbert, fine-tuned DistilBERT and FinBERT), with training data and intended use. Baselines train on PhraseBank AllAgree (2,264 sentences). The fine-tuned transformers train on the Twitter Financial News train split (9,543). The fixed label encoding is negative=0, neutral=1, positive=2.

sections.title: Metrics: in-domain vs OOD
sections.explanation: Reports in-domain test scores together with 5-fold CV macro-F1 (around 0.84), then the OOD benchmark on 2,388 validation headlines. SVM accuracy is 0.67 against a 0.66 majority baseline, with macro-F1 0.46. DistilBERT reaches 0.73 and class-weighted FinBERT reaches 0.84. Showing the majority-class row next to accuracy makes it clear that accuracy alone would overstate the SVM's usefulness.

sections.title: Training data and provenance
sections.explanation: Describes PhraseBank (formal report sentences, ~61% neutral) and the MIT-licensed Twitter set (short ticker-tagged headlines, ~66% neutral), and says the bundled `sample_news.csv` is synthetic and never used for metrics. The domain difference between formal report prose and short headlines is the main explanation for the OOD drop.

sections.title: Intended use and limitations
sections.explanation: States that the project is educational, not financial advice and not a trading signal, and that the LSTM stock demo performs at roughly chance. It lists domain sensitivity, class imbalance (the reason macro-F1 is the primary metric) and the small n=226 test set (with roughly ±3–4% variance, so CV figures are preferred). These are the points an interviewer expects when asking about limitations.

sections.title: Ethics and reproduction
sections.explanation: Notes possible dataset bias, the need for human review before any automated decision, and that no PII is used. It ends with the commands to reproduce the work: train and evaluate baselines, fetch the real dataset and run the generalization evaluation, then fine-tune FinBERT (GPU recommended).

tests/test_generalization.py.overview: An integration test for the real out-of-domain evaluation. It runs `integrate_news.evaluate_generalization('svm')` on the Twitter Financial News set and checks that the returned metrics are valid. It skips cleanly when the dataset has not been fetched or the SVM artifact is missing, so the offline CI suite (tour steps 13 and 14) stays green without large data downloads. Tour step 8 lists it as the test behind the OOD numbers.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Adds `src/` to the path and imports `REAL_NEWS_PATH` and `evaluate_generalization` from `integrate_news`, plus `get_model_dir`. Importing the dataset path constant from the module under test means the skip condition always checks the same file the evaluation reads.

sections.title: Conditional skips and metric checks
sections.explanation: Uses two skip levels: a `skipif` decorator when the dataset file is absent (the reason string gives the fetch command), and an in-test `pytest.skip` when `baseline_svm.joblib` is missing. The assertions check structure and ranges rather than exact scores: positive sample count, accuracy, macro-F1 and majority-class accuracy within [0, 1], and an MIT licence tag in the dataset name. This keeps the test stable across retrains while still catching broken outputs or the wrong dataset.

src/shap_explain.py.overview: Computes global and per-class feature importance for the TF-IDF baseline models and saves them to `results/shap_<model>.json`, with an optional summary plot. The method depends on the model type. Linear models (logreg, SVM) use TF-IDF value × coefficient. Gradient boosting uses a `feature_importances_`-based approximation weighted by predicted probability. Random forest uses SHAP's `TreeExplainer`, and other models fall back to `KernelExplainer`. This is the explainability layer in tour step 9. Its output is displayed on the dashboard but not recomputed there.

sections.title: Module docstring and imports
sections.explanation: Describes the intended explainer per model family. Note that the code below only partly follows the docstring: gradient boosting does not use TreeExplainer in the main path, and linear models compute coefficient products directly instead of calling `shap.LinearExplainer`. `shap` itself is imported inside functions, so the module can be imported without it installed.

sections.title: Loading the pipeline and features
sections.explanation: Imports SHAP lazily with a clear install message, loads `baseline_<model>.joblib`, and takes up to `max_samples` (default 100) rows with a fixed seed, because SHAP can be slow. It extracts the `tfidf` and `classifier` steps from the Pipeline by name, transforms the text, and gets the vocabulary through `get_feature_names_out()`, so importances map back to readable words and bigrams.

sections.title: Choosing the explainer by model type
sections.explanation: This is the core design choice. Random forest tries `TreeExplainer` and, if it fails, falls back to the feature-importance path by adding itself to that set. Gradient boosting skips TreeExplainer (the comment notes multi-class support is unreliable) and approximates per-class contributions as value × global importance × predicted class probability. Linear models use `x_i · coef[c, i]`, which is the exact additive contribution of each feature to the class score (relative to a zero baseline rather than the mean). Any other model falls back to the slow, model-agnostic `KernelExplainer` on a 50-sample background. Interview point: these approximations are faster but less faithful than true SHAP for the tree models.

sections.title: Global and per-class rankings
sections.explanation: Global importance is the mean absolute value over classes and samples (taking abs first, so positive and negative contributions do not cancel), and the top 30 features are kept. When there are three per-class arrays, it also takes the signed mean per class and keeps the top 15 by magnitude, each tagged with a direction. Signed per-class values show which words push towards or away from each sentiment, which is the most useful view for finance users.

sections.title: Saving results
sections.explanation: Runs the explanation and writes it as JSON to `results/shap_<model>.json`, creating the directory if needed. The Generalization and Explainability pages read these files, so the dashboard never pays SHAP's computation cost.

sections.title: Summary plot generation
sections.explanation: Uses the non-interactive `Agg` matplotlib backend so it works on headless servers and in CI. It subsamples up to 200 rows and draws a real `TreeExplainer` summary bar plot (top 20 features) for tree models only, saved at 150 dpi on a white background. Non-tree models get a warning instead of a plot.

sections.title: Command-line interface
sections.explanation: `--model` selects the baseline (default gradient boosting) and `--plot` switches between drawing the summary plot and saving the JSON results; in JSON mode it also prints the top 10 features.

src/explain.py.overview: A lightweight explanation module for the TF-IDF baseline models. It ranks the terms of one sentence by TF-IDF value times the largest classifier coefficient, labels each term's direction using the Loughran-McDonald lexicon first and the model's coefficients second, and also gives a global per-class top-features summary. It is the 'local' explanation behind the Explainability page (tour step 9), and it is cheaper and simpler than the SHAP path in shap_explain.py.

sections.title: Imports and optional lexicon
sections.explanation: The module imports the shared `LABEL_MAP_INV` and model-directory helpers from utils, then tries to import the three lexicon sets. If `lexicons` cannot be imported, it sets `LEXICON_AVAILABLE = False` and swaps in empty sets, so the module still works using coefficients alone. This graceful-degradation pattern shows up across the project wherever an optional dependency or data file is involved.

sections.title: Per-word importance scoring
sections.explanation: This function loads the saved scikit-learn Pipeline and pulls out its `tfidf` and `classifier` steps by name. It then scores only the terms with a non-zero TF-IDF value in this sentence. Importance is `tfidf_value * max(|coef|)` over the three classes, meaning how strongly this word in this sentence moves the model. Direction comes from the financial lexicon first, because a raw coefficient can reflect dataset quirks. Coefficients are the fallback, read with the fixed index layout 0=negative, 1=neutral, 2=positive from `LABEL_MAP`. Classifiers without `coef_` (for example tree models, or a calibrated wrapper) fall back to the plain TF-IDF value with a neutral direction. For bigrams, only the first word is checked against the lexicon. This makes a good interview point about how faithful the explanation really is.

sections.title: Full prediction explanation
sections.explanation: This function builds the dictionary the dashboard renders: the predicted label, probabilities, ranked words, the top words per direction, and raw lexicon hits. If the model has no `predict_proba`, it turns `decision_function` margins into pseudo-probabilities with a numerically stable softmax (subtracting the max first). Lexicon words that the TF-IDF vocabulary missed are added with a small fixed score of 0.1, so out-of-vocabulary finance terms still appear. Note that the pipeline is loaded from disk twice per call (once here and once inside `get_word_importance_baseline`), which is simple but not efficient.

sections.title: HTML highlighting helper
sections.explanation: This function wraps the top 15 important words in coloured `<span>` tags so they can be shown inline. It matches tokens after removing punctuation, so bigram features never match a single token. It also does not HTML-escape the text. The Explainability page uses its own escaped `_highlight` instead, which is the safer version.

sections.title: Global feature summary
sections.explanation: For a linear model with three coefficient rows, this function returns the ten highest-weighted features for each class, using `LABEL_MAP_INV` to name them. It is a global, model-level view, as opposed to the per-sentence view above. Models without `coef_` get an error dictionary instead of an exception.

sections.title: Manual smoke test
sections.explanation: The `__main__` block explains one sample sentence with `baseline_svm` and prints the probabilities and top words. It is a quick manual check, not part of the pytest suite.

src/lexicons.py.overview: A pure-data module that holds the financial word lists, attributed in its docstring to the Loughran-McDonald (2011) dictionary: positive, negative, uncertainty and litigious sets. It was split out of nlp_advanced.py so that explain.py, llm_enhanced.py, nlp_advanced.py and tests can share one source of truth. In tour step 9, these lists give each highlighted word its sentiment direction instead of relying on raw model coefficients.

sections.title: Provenance docstring
sections.explanation: The header cites the Loughran-McDonald paper and its dictionary URL. That matters in interviews, because general-purpose sentiment lexicons misclassify finance words (for example 'liability' or 'tax'), and LM was built specifically from 10-K filings.

sections.title: Positive word set
sections.explanation: `FINANCIAL_POSITIVE` is a Python `set`, so membership checks are O(1) during per-word explanation. It lists inflected forms explicitly (achieve, achieved, achieves, achieving) instead of stemming, which keeps lookup trivial. From line 85 it adds project-specific 'growth/comparison indicators' such as 'up', 'more' and 'boost', and 'earnings' also appears in this set. These are extensions beyond the original LM list, tuned for headline phrasing. They are also a source of bias: 'earnings' on its own is not positive.

sections.title: Negative word set
sections.explanation: `FINANCIAL_NEGATIVE` is by far the largest list. This matches the LM finding that financial text has many more negative than positive terms. explain.py checks it right after the positive set, so a word in both sets would resolve as positive.

sections.title: Uncertainty and litigious sets
sections.explanation: `FINANCIAL_UNCERTAINTY` (for example 'volatile', 'volatility') and `FINANCIAL_LITIGIOUS` (for example 'allege', 'tribunal', 'verdict') are not sentiment classes in the three-label scheme. They are extra signals: explain.py reports uncertainty hits separately, and nlp_advanced.py uses the litigious set. Keeping them as separate sets lets callers treat risk language differently from plain negativity.

app/views/3_Explainability.py.overview: The Streamlit page that shows explainability for the TF-IDF baselines. The top half is a local explanation of one sentence from `explain_prediction_baseline`, shown as a verdict card, a tinted sentence and a term table. The bottom half is a global explanation from precomputed SHAP results in `results/shap_<clf>.json`, which can be computed on demand. It is the user-facing end of tour step 9 and is honest about scope: transformer models are told up front that this page does not apply to them.

sections.title: Imports and optional SHAP
sections.explanation: The page adds `src/` to `sys.path` so it can import project modules directly, and it treats `shap_explain` as optional through a try/except that sets `SHAP_AVAILABLE`. All styling helpers come from the shared `shared` module, so every page uses the same design system.

sections.title: Model gate and examples
sections.explanation: `active_model()` reads the model chosen in the sidebar. If it is not a `baseline_*` model, the page shows an info banner and calls `st.stop()`. TF-IDF-weight-times-coefficient attribution and the linear/tree SHAP explainers only make sense for vocabulary-based models, and refusing is better than showing a misleading explanation for FinBERT.
