The `EXAMPLES` dictionary gives one-click demo sentences.

sections.title: Safe highlighting
sections.explanation: `_use_example` is a widget callback that copies the chosen example into session state and sets a run flag, so choosing a pill both fills the text box and triggers an explanation. `_highlight` tokenises with a regex that keeps whitespace and punctuation, so the original spacing is preserved. It skips bigrams and HTML-escapes every token before wrapping matches in `<mark>`. The class is shown by both tint and underline colour, plus a hover title, so the meaning does not depend on colour alone. This is an accessibility choice.

sections.title: Local explanation flow
sections.explanation: The input widgets are a pill selector, a text area and a button. `run` is true either on a click or when the callback's `ex_run` flag is popped. Empty input shows a warning, and errors inside `explain_prediction_baseline` are caught and shown as a banner instead of crashing the page. The output combines a verdict card with the top probability, the highlighted sentence, a term-attribution table of the top 10 terms, and Loughran-McDonald lexicon matches. A `source_note` cites the exact model file used.

sections.title: Global SHAP chart
sections.explanation: This section loads `results/shap_<classifier>.json` if it exists, and treats a parse failure (for example an un-fetched Git LFS pointer) as 'no data'. It plots the top 20 features by mean |SHAP| as a horizontal bar chart. The caption points out that function words rank highly, which suggests the model learned PhraseBank's phrasing. That is the same overfitting story as the out-of-domain results. A three-column table then lists signed per-class SHAP values.

sections.title: On-demand SHAP fallback
sections.explanation: If no saved file exists but SHAP is installed, a button computes explanations for 100 samples, writes the JSON to `results/` and calls `st.rerun()` so the chart path above renders it. If SHAP is not installed, the page shows an install hint. Caching the expensive computation to disk keeps later page loads instant.

src/llm_provider.py.overview: A small factory that decides which LLM vendor and model to use (Anthropic Claude, OpenRouter or OpenAI) from arguments and environment variables, and returns a LangChain chat model. Everything above it (the benchmark, RAG, the Ask the News page) depends only on this interface, so the vendor is a configuration choice and not a code change. This is the 'vendor-agnostic' layer described in tour step 10.

sections.title: Resolution rules and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring states the full precedence: provider comes from `FINSIGHT_LLM_PROVIDER`, else whichever API key is present (in a fixed order), else anthropic. Model comes from the argument, then the env var, then the provider default. Temperature defaults to 0. Only Anthropic has a default model (a Haiku-tier id, chosen as the cheapest and fastest for classification). OpenRouter and OpenAI deliberately have none, so you must choose a model explicitly instead of silently paying for an expensive one.

sections.title: Provider, model and temperature resolvers
sections.explanation: `get_provider` normalises and validates the name, raising `ValueError` for unknown providers so a typo fails early. `get_model_name` raises an error with an actionable message when no model is configured. `get_temperature` lets `FINSIGHT_LLM_TEMPERATURE=none` remove the parameter entirely for models that reject it. `has_api_key` lets callers check for credentials before making any network call.

sections.title: Chat model factory
sections.explanation: This function builds a shared kwargs dictionary (model, timeout, max_retries, and temperature if set), then lazily imports the matching LangChain class. Lazy imports mean only the installed vendor package is needed. OpenRouter reuses `ChatOpenAI`, because OpenRouter exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, with a different base URL, the OpenRouter key and an `X-Title` header that names the app. `max_tokens` is a parameter, so classification can request 64 tokens while RAG answers request 600.

sections.title: Structured output binding
sections.explanation: This function wraps LangChain's `with_structured_output` with one provider-specific choice: for OpenRouter it forces `method="function_calling"`, because tool calling is supported by more of the vendors OpenRouter routes to than JSON-schema mode. `include_raw` is passed through so the benchmark can read token usage from the raw message.

src/llm_sentiment.py.overview: Core logic for benchmarking an LLM as a three-way financial sentiment classifier against fine-tuned FinBERT (tour step 10). It defines the prompt, a Pydantic output schema, leakage-free few-shot examples, a disk cache of answers, a concurrent classify loop, and a cost/latency summary. The design choices (constrained labels, temperature 0, caching, invalid answers counted as wrong) all serve the goal of a fair, repeatable comparison.

sections.title: Design docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring states the research question (does a general LLM beat a small fine-tuned model, and at what cost?) and the design rules. `get_model_name`, `make_chat_model` and `with_structured_output` are re-exported from `llm_provider`, which is why the `# noqa: F401` is there. The benchmark script imports `get_model_name` from this module.

sections.title: Prompt and output schema
sections.explanation: `PROMPT_VERSION` is part of the cache key, so editing the prompt and bumping the version stops stale answers from being reused. The system prompt defines each label from an investor's point of view, which reduces ambiguity for headlines such as 'company cuts costs'. `SentimentLabel` uses `Literal[...]`, so structured output can only return one of the three labels. Anything else becomes a parsing failure that is counted, not silently coerced.

sections.title: Leakage-free few-shot examples
sections.explanation: This function samples `per_class` examples per label from the PhraseBank training split with a fixed seed. Taking them from training data and never from the 2,388 evaluation headlines prevents test leakage. The final list comprehension interleaves the classes (neg, neu, pos, neg, ...), so the model cannot infer the answer from a run of same-label examples.

sections.title: Message construction and runnable
sections.explanation: This builds chat messages as `(role, content)` tuples. Few-shot mode adds each example as a prior human turn plus an AI reply, so the model sees worked dialogue and not one long instruction. `make_runnable` asks for only 64 output tokens and `include_raw=True`, so token usage stays available for cost reporting.

sections.title: Content-addressed answer cache
sections.explanation: The cache key is a SHA-256 of model, prompt version, mode and text. `AnswerCache` is an append-only JSON-lines file loaded into a dictionary at startup. Appending is crash-safe and cheap: a run that is interrupted part-way keeps every answer written so far. The key does not include the few-shot example set or the provider, so it relies on examples being deterministic (fixed seed) and on model ids being distinct.

sections.title: Single call with error capture
sections.explanation: This function times one `invoke`, catches any exception and returns it as a record instead of raising, so one failure does not abort a 2,388-call benchmark. It handles both the `{parsed, raw}` dictionary from `include_raw` and a plain parsed object. Tokens are read from `usage_metadata`. A missing or invalid label becomes `None`, together with the parsing error, and is later scored as wrong.

sections.title: Concurrent classification
sections.explanation: This function first resolves cache hits (only valid labels count as hits), then sends the remaining texts to a `ThreadPoolExecutor`. Threads suit this workload because it is I/O-bound network calls. `pool.map` returns results in input order, and writing into a pre-sized `results` list keeps alignment with the texts. Only valid answers are cached, so a re-run automatically retries failures.

sections.title: Usage and cost summary
sections.explanation: This function totals input and output tokens and computes cost only when the caller supplies prices, returning `None` instead of a guessed number. It reports p50 and p95 latency, including the stored latency of cached answers, plus counts of invalid answers, errors and cached reuse. Token totals include cached records, so `cost_usd` estimates what the full run costs and not only what this invocation spent. The docstring's mention of OpenAI's pricing page predates multi-provider support.

scripts/llm_benchmark.py.overview: The command-line driver that runs the LLM sentiment benchmark on the 2,388 real Twitter financial headlines and writes `results/llm_benchmark.json` for the Generalization page. It reuses llm_sentiment for prompting and caching and stats.bootstrap_macro_f1 for the metric, so the LLM number is directly comparable to FinBERT's (tour steps 7 and 10). It adds safeguards against cost: a dry-run mode, stratified sampling and early exit when every call fails.

sections.title: Usage docstring
sections.explanation: The docstring documents a three-stage workflow: `--dry-run` (see the prompts and a token estimate for free), `--limit 200` (a cheap trial) and a full run with prices. It also shows how to switch provider. Putting the cost-safe path first is deliberate for a benchmark that spends real money.

sections.title: Imports and constants
sections.explanation: The script resolves the project root and puts `src/` on `sys.path`, then imports provider helpers, the llm_sentiment API and `bootstrap_macro_f1`. `DATA`, `CACHE` and `DATASET` fix the evaluation file, the answer cache location and the dataset citation that is written into the results.

sections.title: Stratified loading and dry run
sections.explanation: `load_eval` uses `groupby('label').sample(frac=...)` so a `--limit` trial keeps the real class mix and its macro-F1 is meaningful. `dry_run` prints the exact messages for each mode and estimates prompt tokens with a 4-characters-per-token rule. It warns that the schema/tool definition sent with each call can make the billed total several times higher.

sections.title: CLI arguments and preflight
sections.explanation: argparse exposes provider, model, modes, limit, prices, concurrency and dry-run. Before creating a runnable, the script resolves provider and model and exits with a clear message if the API key is missing. `full_set` records whether this run used all rows, so a sample is never mistaken for the headline number.

sections.title: Per-mode scoring loop
sections.explanation: For each mode the script classifies, aborts if every call failed (usually a bad key, a wrong model id or no credit), and maps labels to ids. Invalid answers become `-1`, which can never equal a true label, so they count as wrong. It computes accuracy, a bootstrap macro-F1 CI, a confusion matrix with fixed labels [0,1,2] and the usage summary. The three most common error messages are printed, and the script notes that failures are not cached and will be retried.

sections.title: Results file
sections.explanation: The script writes provider, model, prompt version, dataset, n, `full_set`, prices, a UTC timestamp and the per-mode runs to `results/llm_benchmark.json`. Recording all of this makes the result reproducible and auditable. A sample run prints a reminder to run on the full set before comparing with FinBERT on identical rows.

src/rag_news.py.overview: Retrieval-augmented question answering over the 2,388 real headlines (tour step 10). It embeds headlines into a LangChain `InMemoryVectorStore`, by default with local TF-IDF+LSA embeddings and optionally with OpenAI embeddings. It retrieves the top-k matches, asks a chat model for a structured answer with citations, and drops any citation outside the retrieved set. The module is written to be grounded, cheap and safe against prompt injection hidden in headlines.

sections.title: Pipeline docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring describes the four-step pipeline and explains why embeddings are local by default: they are free, instant and need no second key, and Anthropic has no embeddings API. It also states that headlines are treated as untrusted data. Chat models come from `llm_provider`, so RAG is vendor-agnostic like the benchmark.

sections.title: Constants, prompt and schema
sections.explanation: `QUESTION_WORDS` adds words such as 'news' and 'saying' to the stop words, because they appear in questions and would otherwise dominate retrieval. The system prompt requires answers from the headlines only, numbered citations, a fixed `NOT_FOUND` sentence, ignoring instructions inside headlines, no claims about the present, and under 120 words. `NewsAnswer` makes the model return `answer` plus a list of integer `citations`, which the code can then check.

sections.title: Embedding configuration
sections.explanation: These helpers resolve `FINSIGHT_EMBEDDINGS` (local or openai) and the embedding model name. Local embeddings always report the fixed name `local-tfidf-lsa`, which is also used in the index cache filename.

sections.title: Local LSA embeddings
sections.explanation: This class is classic latent semantic analysis: TF-IDF over unigrams and bigrams with sublinear TF and a token pattern that keeps cashtags like `$TSLA`, then `TruncatedSVD` down to at most 256 dimensions (capped by the matrix shape), then L2 normalisation. After normalisation, dot product equals cosine similarity, and the zero-norm guard avoids division by zero for queries made only of stop words. It implements LangChain's `Embeddings` duck-typed interface, including async methods, so it plugs into the vector store directly. The fixed SVD seed makes it reproducible.

sections.title: Corpus loading and index caching
sections.explanation: `load_corpus` gives each headline a stable integer id from its row number. `_index_path` puts both the embedding model name and a hash of the corpus in the cache filename, so changing either one invalidates the saved index automatically. `build_index` loads a dumped store if one exists. Otherwise it adds texts with id and gold-label metadata and saves to disk, so paid API embeddings are computed only once.

sections.title: Retrieval and prompt building
sections.explanation: `retrieve` calls `similarity_search_with_score` and numbers the hits from 1 to k. These numbers are what the model cites, which is easier and harder to hallucinate than raw ids. `build_messages` puts the numbered headlines and the question into one human turn after the system prompt.

sections.title: Runnable and embedding factories
sections.explanation: `make_answer_runnable` builds a chat model with 600 max tokens and 2 retries and binds the `NewsAnswer` schema. `make_embeddings` returns the local LSA embedder fitted on the corpus, or lazily imports `OpenAIEmbeddings`, so `langchain_openai` is needed only when OpenAI embeddings are used.

sections.title: Citation-validated answering
sections.explanation: `answer_question` rejects empty questions and short-circuits to `NOT_FOUND` when nothing was retrieved, which costs nothing. After the call it removes duplicate citations while keeping their order (`dict.fromkeys`). It then splits them into valid citations and `dropped_citations` that point outside the sources, and reports the dropped ones instead of hiding them. `sentiment_mix` computes the label shares of the retrieved headlines so the UI can check the answer's tone against its evidence.

app/views/10_Ask_the_News.py.overview: The Streamlit page for the RAG feature from rag_news.py (tour step 10). It resolves LLM and embedding settings from environment variables or Streamlit secrets, checks for the needed API keys, caches the vector store and the answer runnable, then shows a cited answer, the sentiment mix of the evidence as scored by the active FinSight model, and a sources table. It stops early with a helpful state at every precondition that can fail.

sections.title: Imports and model check
sections.explanation: The page puts `src/` and `app/` on the path, imports the shared UI helpers and gets the active model. It stops if no predictor loaded, because each retrieved headline is scored by that model. The header states the corpus and that it has no dates, which sets expectations up front.

sections.title: Settings from env or secrets
sections.explanation: `_setting` reads an environment variable first and falls back to `st.secrets`. When it finds a secret it copies it into `os.environ`, because the LangChain clients and `llm_provider` read from the environment. Looping over every relevant key makes Streamlit Cloud secrets work with no extra code path.

sections.title: Dependency and key preflight
sections.explanation: If the LangChain imports fail, the page shows an install command. Configuration `ValueError`s (unknown provider, missing model) are shown escaped. The page then lists exactly which keys are missing: the chat provider's key, plus `OPENAI_API_KEY` only when OpenAI embeddings are used with a different chat provider. It also tells the user that search is local, so each question costs one chat call.

sections.title: Cached store and answerer
sections.explanation: `@st.cache_resource` keeps the vector store and the runnable alive across reruns and sessions, keyed by their arguments. Only OpenAI embeddings are saved to disk, because the local LSA index rebuilds in seconds. Writing it to disk would only add stale-cache risk.

sections.title: Question form
sections.explanation: Example questions are offered as pills. An `on_change` callback copies the chosen pill into the text input's session key. The `st.form` groups the question and the k slider so the page reruns only on submit. Without a submit, or with a blank question, the page stops early.

sections.title: Retrieve, score, answer
sections.explanation: The page retrieves k sources, scores each headline with the active FinSight predictor in one batch call, and asks the LLM for a grounded answer. Any failure (network, auth, rate limit) is caught and shown as a truncated, escaped error banner instead of a traceback.

sections.title: Answer and citation warnings
sections.explanation: The answer is HTML-escaped first, and then `[n]` markers are turned into superscripts. Escaping before adding markup prevents injection from model output. The page warns when an answer that is not `NOT_FOUND` has no citations, and when citations were dropped because they pointed at headlines that were not retrieved.

sections.title: Evidence sentiment and sources
sections.explanation: A probability band shows the sentiment mix of the retrieved headlines, so users can compare the tone of the answer with its evidence. The sources table marks cited rows and shows the model label next to the human gold label (exposing model errors) plus the similarity score. The closing note says that answers describe the dataset, not today's market.

api/main.py.overview: The FastAPI inference service from tour step 11. It wraps the same `SentimentPredictor` the dashboard uses behind /health, /models, /predict, /predict/batch and /metrics. Around that core it adds Pydantic validation, optional API-key auth, slowapi rate limiting (with in-memory or Redis storage), a timing middleware, structured audit logging and a per-process predictor cache. Configuration comes from environment variables, so one image works in local, Docker Compose and cloud deployments.

sections.title: Service docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the endpoints and features. `src/` is put on `sys.path` so the API imports `predict` and `monitoring` directly, without packaging. Reusing the dashboard's predictor means the API and the UI cannot drift apart in preprocessing or label mapping.

sections.title: Environment configuration
sections.explanation: Defaults (model, maximum text length, maximum batch size, rate limits) can all be overridden through `FINSIGHT_*` environment variables, following twelve-factor config. `FINSIGHT_REDIS_URL` moves rate-limit counters into Redis so they are shared across workers and replicas. `TRUST_PROXY` is off by default because X-Forwarded-For can be spoofed by clients.

sections.title: Client key and API-key auth
sections.explanation: `_client_key` uses the first X-Forwarded-For hop only when the proxy is explicitly trusted (for example nginx in docker-compose), and otherwise uses the socket address. `require_api_key` is a FastAPI dependency that reads `FINSIGHT_API_KEY` on every call, not at import time. Auth can therefore be toggled per deployment and in tests without re-importing the app. Failures increment a metric and return 401.

sections.title: Limiter, app and predictor cache
sections.explanation: The slowapi `Limiter` uses Redis storage when configured, otherwise `memory://`. Startup warnings make the insecure defaults (no auth, per-process limits) visible in the logs. `_PREDICTORS` caches loaded models per worker process, so heavy weights load once and not on every request. The cache key is the client-supplied model name and the dictionary has no lock, so a concurrent first request could load a model twice. That outcome is wasteful but harmless.

sections.title: Request and response schemas
sections.explanation: `PredictRequest` enforces 1 to MAX_TEXT_CHARS characters and rejects whitespace-only text. `BatchPredictRequest` caps the list size and checks each item's length. It also silently drops blank entries, so the returned `count` can be smaller than the number submitted. `PredictResponse` fixes the response contract that is shown in the OpenAPI docs.

sections.title: Rate-limit handler and timing middleware
sections.explanation: The 429 handler counts and logs rate-limited calls. The HTTP middleware counts every request, records latency into the metrics registry, adds an `X-Process-Time-ms` header, and turns unexpected exceptions into a generic 500 that does not leak internals. The handler logs the raw remote address even when the proxy is trusted.

sections.title: Health and model listing
sections.explanation: `/health` serves as a liveness probe (used by the Docker healthcheck) and also reports the default model, the available models, whether auth is enabled and which rate-limit backend is active. These endpoints have no auth or rate-limit decorators, so orchestrators can always reach them.

sections.title: Single and batch prediction
sections.explanation: Both endpoints require the API key and have separate rate limits, with batch limited more strictly because it does more work per call. slowapi needs the `request: Request` parameter. They are plain `def` functions, so FastAPI runs them in a threadpool, which is why the metrics registry uses a lock. A missing model maps to 400 and other failures to 500. Successful calls update counters, including per-label counts that support drift monitoring, and write a structured audit event that records text length but not the text itself.

sections.title: Metrics endpoint
sections.explanation: `/metrics` returns the registry snapshot (uptime, counters, latency percentiles) behind the API key. The numbers are per process, so with several replicas each one reports its own figures. A production setup would usually scrape these into Prometheus or a similar system.

src/monitoring.py.overview: A stdlib-only monitoring module for the API (tour step 11). It provides a console logger, a best-effort JSON-lines audit trail at `logs/predictions.jsonl`, and a thread-safe in-process metrics registry with a bounded latency window and percentile reporting. It has no dependencies so it runs on any deploy target, at the cost of metrics that are per process and reset on restart.

sections.title: Purpose and paths
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the design goal: no dependencies, so it runs on constrained targets. The log directory is resolved relative to the repository root, and predictions are appended to `logs/predictions.jsonl`.

sections.title: Idempotent logger setup
sections.explanation: This section creates a named `finsight.api` logger and attaches a stream handler only if none exists. The guard prevents duplicate log lines when the module is imported more than once (for example on uvicorn reload or in tests).

sections.title: Structured audit events
sections.explanation: `log_event` writes one JSON object per line with a UTC ISO timestamp and arbitrary keyword fields. `default=str` handles non-serialisable values. Every exception is swallowed, because observability must never break a user request. JSON lines are easy to append to and easy to ship to log pipelines.

sections.title: Thread-safe metrics registry
sections.explanation: Counters and a `deque(maxlen=1000)` of latencies are protected by a `threading.Lock`, because FastAPI runs sync endpoints in a threadpool. The bounded deque keeps memory constant and makes percentiles reflect recent traffic. `snapshot` copies the data under the lock and computes p50, p95 and p99 outside it, using nearest-rank on the sorted window, so lock hold time stays short.

sections.title: Module singleton
sections.explanation: A single `metrics` instance is shared by everything that imports the module. This is a simple process-wide registry, and it explains why each worker or replica has its own independent numbers.

src/registry.py.overview: A lightweight model registry (tour step 11 and the retraining workflow). It finds trained artifacts, hashes them, adds their latest evaluation metrics, and writes a snapshot to `models/registry.json`. MLflow logging is optional. It gives reviewable model lineage without running a tracking server.

sections.title: Docstring and setup
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the goal: reproducible lineage with no infrastructure, plus optional MLflow integration. `REGISTRY_PATH` sits next to the models, so the registry is versioned in git together with them.

sections.title: Artifact hashing
sections.explanation: The function streams the file in 8 KB chunks into SHA-256, so large models never have to fit in memory, and keeps 12 hex characters as a short fingerprint. Comparing hashes shows whether a retrain actually changed an artifact.

sections.title: Loading evaluation metrics
sections.explanation: This function reads `results/evaluation_results.json` defensively. A missing file, invalid JSON or a non-list payload all return an empty mapping instead of crashing. It keeps accuracy, macro-F1 and weighted-F1 keyed by model name.

sections.title: Discovery and snapshot build
sections.explanation: Discovery covers `baseline_*.joblib` and, if present, LSTM `.pt` files from the stock-prediction extension. Fine-tuned transformer weights are not included in this registry. Each entry records name, filename, hash, size, modification time and the matching metrics, and the snapshot is stamped with a generation time and a count.

sections.title: Write and MLflow
sections.explanation: `update_registry` writes the JSON snapshot. `log_to_mlflow` imports MLflow lazily and returns False with a warning if it is missing. Otherwise it creates one run per model with the hash and artifact as tags, size as a param and numeric metrics. This keeps MLflow an optional add-on and not a hard dependency.

sections.title: Command-line interface
sections.explanation: `--update` rebuilds the registry and prints it, `--mlflow` implies an update, and `--show` prints the saved file. The retrain workflow calls this to refresh lineage after training.

app/app.py.overview: The Streamlit entry point and router (tour step 12). It sets page config once, registers the dashboard pages with `st.navigation` grouped into Overview, Analyze, Explain, Evaluate and Labs, injects the shared CSS, renders the sidebar once and runs the selected page. Because the sidebar lives in the router, the model selection persists across pages, and each page reads it through `shared.active_model()`.

sections.title: Path setup and page config
sections.explanation: Both `src/` and `app/` are added to `sys.path` so pages can import model code and the shared UI module. `st.set_page_config` must be the first Streamlit call, which is why `shared` is imported only after it (hence `noqa: E402`). The layout is wide and the favicon is a local SVG.

sections.title: Page factory
sections.explanation: `_page` is a small helper that builds an `st.Page` from a file path relative to the app directory, with a title, a Material icon and an explicit `url_path`. Explicit URL paths give stable deep links even when page titles change. For example, the 'Generalization' page keeps the `Sentiment_Trends` path from its filename.

sections.title: Grouped page registry
sections.explanation: `PAGES` maps section names to page lists, and `st.navigation` renders them as grouped sidebar navigation. This version registers eleven pages, with Home as the default. Grouping by user task (analyze, explain, evaluate) follows the project's story, from making predictions to understanding them to checking them.

sections.title: Router run
sections.explanation: The router builds the navigation, injects the global CSS once, draws the shared sidebar (brand and model selector), then runs the selected page. Rendering the sidebar here instead of in every page avoids duplicated widgets and keeps the selection in one place.

app/ui.py.overview: ui.py is the dashboard's design system and model loader. It defines colour tokens, global CSS, a default Plotly theme and reusable HTML components (page masthead, numbered exhibits, KPI strips, verdict card with a probability band, term tables, interval charts). It also owns model loading and the persistent sidebar: `load_predictor` returns either the in-process `SentimentPredictor` or the HTTP `RemotePredictor`, depending on whether `FINSIGHT_API_URL` is set. This is the UI/serving split described in tour step 12. Pages import these helpers through the `shared` module instead of importing ui.py directly.

sections.title: Module purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring sets out the design rules: white report background, hairline rules instead of card shadows, numbered exhibits with a source line, and sentiment that is never shown by colour alone (each label gets a glyph and a word, for accessibility). It puts `src/` on `sys.path` so any page that triggers this import can reach `predict.SentimentPredictor` and `get_available_models`. Native widgets are themed in `.streamlit/config.toml`, so this file only styles the HTML that Streamlit does not draw itself.

sections.title: Design tokens and small helpers
sections.explanation: `COLORS`, `SENTIMENT_COLORS`, `SENTIMENT_TINTS` and `SENTIMENT_GLYPHS` are the single source of truth for the palette, so every page looks the same. `MODEL_LABELS` maps internal keys such as `baseline_svm` to display names, and `model_label` builds a readable name for any key it does not know. `load_result` reads `results/*.json` under `st.cache_data` and returns `None` on any failure, including an un-fetched Git LFS pointer. Pages can then fall back gracefully instead of crashing.

sections.title: Inline SVG icon set
sections.explanation: Streamlit cannot place Material Symbols inside custom HTML, so a small set of hand-written SVG paths is kept here. `icon()` wraps them in an SVG whose stroke uses `currentColor`. A banner's CSS class can therefore recolour the icon without touching the markup. Icons are marked `aria-hidden` because the text beside them carries the meaning.

sections.title: Global CSS and injection
sections.explanation: `BASE_CSS` defines CSS custom properties that mirror the Python tokens, then styles the sidebar shell, masthead, section headings, key-figure rows, banners, empty states, the verdict band and term tables. It includes a `max-width: 760px` media query for phone layouts. Legacy class names (`metric-card`, `insight-card`) are restyled rather than removed, so older pages still render in the new style. `inject_css()` is called once per run by the router.

sections.title: Plotly report theme
sections.explanation: `_register_template` builds a `finsight` template from `plotly_white` and makes it Plotly's global default. Even charts nobody styles explicitly then match the report. `style_fig` applies the same theme to a single figure, with options for height and title. `render_chart` passes `theme=None` so Streamlit's own chart theme does not override the template, and it hides the mode bar.

sections.title: Layout components
sections.explanation: These helpers emit HTML for the report structure. `page_header` resets a per-page exhibit counter in `st.session_state`, and `exhibit` increments it, so exhibit numbers restart on every page. `kpi_strip` colours a value only when its accent is a sentiment colour, which keeps colour meaningful. `status_banner` and `empty_state` replace the default Streamlit alerts. The `_svg = icon` alias exists because `empty_state` has a parameter called `icon` that shadows the function.

sections.title: Verdict card and term table
sections.explanation: `probability_band` draws the class probabilities as one segmented bar. The predicted class is solid and the others are tinted, so the spread of the model's belief is visible at a glance. A minimum width keeps tiny probabilities visible. `verdict_card` combines glyph, word, confidence and band, and escapes the label with `html.escape`. `term_table` normalises bar widths by the largest absolute weight and escapes each term, which matters because the terms come from user-supplied text. `chart_container` is a small context manager that adds an exhibit heading before a chart.

sections.title: Sentiment and interval charts
sections.explanation: `create_probability_chart` and `create_gauge_chart` are simple Plotly views of one prediction. `interval_chart` is the dot-and-interval chart used for bootstrap results: for each row it draws a translucent band from `low` to `high`, end caps, a point estimate with a hover template, and a label above the band rather than in a left margin, so the chart keeps its full width on a phone. An optional dotted reference line marks a baseline such as "always neutral". This is how the dashboard shows uncertainty instead of single point scores.

sections.title: Local vs remote predictor
sections.explanation: `load_predictor` is the switch between the two serving modes. If `FINSIGHT_API_URL` is set, it lazily imports `api_client.RemotePredictor` and passes the optional `FINSIGHT_API_KEY`. Otherwise it builds an in-process `SentimentPredictor`. `st.cache_resource` keeps one loaded model per key across reruns and sessions, which avoids reloading heavy weights. `_list_models` asks the API's `/models` endpoint in split mode and falls back to the local model list if that call returns nothing.

sections.title: Persistent sidebar and active_model
sections.explanation: `setup_sidebar` runs once per script run from the `app.py` router, so the selected model stays the same across page switches. It defaults to `baseline_svm`, the fast, well-calibrated model. It shows a ready/unavailable status, the model family, and a note on what data the model was trained on, which keeps the UI honest about each model's limits. A loading failure is caught and shown in the sidebar instead of crashing the app. The `(model, predictor)` pair goes into `st.session_state`, and pages read it with `active_model()`, which shows an empty state and calls `st.stop()` when no model is loaded.

app/api_client.py.overview: api_client.py is a thin HTTP client that lets the Streamlit UI get predictions from the FastAPI inference service instead of loading models in-process. `RemotePredictor` copies the `predict()` signature of `SentimentPredictor`, so pages work the same whether inference is local or remote. ui.load_predictor activates it when `FINSIGHT_API_URL` is set. The UI then becomes a stateless presentation layer, and the model service can scale on its own (tour step 12).

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring states the design goal: separate presentation from inference so that the model service can scale behind a load balancer. The only dependency is `httpx`, a lightweight HTTP client, so the UI container does not need torch or scikit-learn when it runs in split mode.

sections.title: Error type
sections.explanation: `RemotePredictorError` subclasses `RuntimeError` so callers can tell network or service failures apart from other bugs. Pages already wrap `predict()` in a broad try/except and show the message in a banner, so a clear error string is what reaches the user.

sections.title: RemotePredictor and _post
sections.explanation: The constructor strips any trailing slash from the base URL, sends the `X-API-Key` header only when a key is configured, and stores a timeout (30 s by default) so a hung service cannot freeze the UI. `_post` turns transport errors (`httpx.HTTPError`) and any non-200 status into `RemotePredictorError`. It trims the response body to 200 characters so error messages stay readable. Using `raise ... from exc` keeps the original traceback.

sections.title: Single and batch predict
sections.explanation: `predict` accepts either one string or a list, just like the local predictor. A string goes to `/predict`, and a list goes to `/predict/batch`, from which the `results` array is returned. Sending a whole list in one request avoids one HTTP round trip per sentence when the batch page scores a file. Because the interface matches the local one, this is a drop-in replacement (duck typing) rather than a shared base class.

sections.title: Remote model discovery
sections.explanation: `remote_available_models` calls `/models` with a shorter 10 s timeout and returns an empty list on any failure. It never raises. ui._list_models treats the empty list as a signal to fall back to locally available models, so the sidebar still renders when the API is down.

app/home.py.overview: home.py is the dashboard's front page, written like the cover of a report. Every headline number (test macro-F1, 5-fold CV, real-news OOD score, fine-tuned FinBERT score and their bootstrap intervals) is read from `results/*.json`, with hard-coded fallbacks used only when an artifact is missing. The page therefore cannot drift away from the evaluation outputs. It tells the project's central story: 0.90 in-domain, 0.46 on real news, recovered to 0.84 with domain fine-tuning. It also links to every analysis page (tour step 12).

sections.title: Imports from shared
sections.explanation: The page adds both `src/` and `app/` to `sys.path`, then imports its components from `shared`, which re-exports the helpers in ui.py. Pages depend on that one interface, and test_page_imports.py checks that each imported name really exists.

sections.title: headline_numbers with fallbacks
sections.explanation: The function starts from a dict of known-good default values, then overwrites them from `cv_results.json`, `model_comparison_ood.json` and `bootstrap_ci.json` wherever those files are available. The walrus operator (`:=`) keeps the optional lookups short. It also derives the macro-F1 of always predicting "neutral" analytically: F1 on the neutral class is 2p/(1+p) where p is the majority-class accuracy, and the other two classes score 0, so the total is divided by 3. That gives a meaningful floor for the chart's reference line.

sections.title: Masthead, call to action and KPI strip
sections.explanation: The masthead's subtitle, "measured honestly", announces the page's angle. A primary button goes straight to Single Analysis using `st.switch_page`. The four key figures pair each score with its context: the CI for FinBERT, accuracy against the majority baseline for the SVM, ± std for CV, and the OOD sample size. A bare number without that context could look better than it is.

sections.title: Exhibit: macro-F1 with intervals
sections.explanation: This exhibit is the central finding as a single chart: three dot-and-interval rows (SVM on the PhraseBank test, SVM on real news, fine-tuned FinBERT on real news), with a dotted reference line for always predicting "neutral". The source note names the artifacts and the resample count. It also states that FinBERT was fine-tuned on the news training split, so its row is a held-out in-domain result, not an out-of-domain one. That caveat heads off a common interview challenge.

sections.title: What happened narrative
sections.explanation: Three columns tell the project story: train a strong baseline, stress-test it on real news (SHAP shows it relying on stopwords from annual-report phrasing), then fix it with domain data. The numbers are interpolated from `n`, so the text stays consistent with the results files.

sections.title: Contents grid
sections.explanation: `CONTENTS` is a data table of (path, title, icon, description) for each analysis page, rendered as `st.page_link` entries. The loop builds the grid row by row (three columns at a time) instead of column by column. On a phone, where columns stack, the links then still read in order. The Stock Prediction entry is labelled experimental and chance-level, which keeps the UI honest about its limits.

app/views/1_Single_Analysis.py.overview: This is the main page: it scores one financial sentence and shows the verdict, confidence, the full probability band and the words that drove the decision. It gets the active model from the sidebar through `active_model()` and calls the shared `predict()` interface, so it works the same with local or remote inference. For TF-IDF baselines it adds term-level drivers and a rationale built from a template. For transformers it points users to the Explainability page instead (tour step 12).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The page imports `explain_prediction_baseline` and `get_llm_explanation` from `src/` and its UI components from `shared`. The `sys.path` changes are needed because Streamlit runs each page as a script rather than as a package module.

sections.title: Model guard and header
sections.explanation: `active_model()` returns the sidebar's selection. The page also calls `st.stop()` if the predictor is `None`, an extra guard so nothing below runs without a model. Streamlit pages execute from top to bottom on every interaction, so stopping early is the normal way to guard a page.

sections.title: Safe bold rendering and examples
sections.explanation: `_md_bold` HTML-escapes the whole string first and only then turns `**bold**` into `<b>`. Text that reaches `unsafe_allow_html` therefore cannot inject markup, a small XSS safeguard. The example pills use an `on_change` callback that writes the example text into the text area's session key and sets a `sa_run` flag. Choosing an example then fills the input and runs the analysis in a single click.

sections.title: Input and trigger logic
sections.explanation: The analyse trigger is true if the button was clicked or if the `sa_run` flag set by an example is present. `st.session_state.pop` clears that flag, so it fires only once. Before any analysis the page shows an explanatory empty state. Blank input produces a warning instead of a call to the model.

sections.title: Prediction and baseline explanation
sections.explanation: The prediction runs inside a spinner, and any exception, local or remote, is shown as an error banner followed by `st.stop()`. The result is read defensively: `confidence` and `probabilities` use `.get`, because some models do not expose probabilities. A word-level explanation is computed only for `baseline_` models, since it relies on TF-IDF weights times model coefficients. Its failures are swallowed so that a missing explanation never blocks the verdict.

sections.title: Result layout and rationale
sections.explanation: The left column shows the verdict card with the probability band, plus a note when a model has no probabilities. The right column lists the top six key drivers, or explains how to see drivers for other models. The "Why this verdict" text is labelled as a template built from word weights, "not an LLM", which is honest about where the explanation comes from. It is passed through `_md_bold` before rendering.

tests/test_api.py.overview: test_api.py tests the FastAPI inference service in-process with FastAPI's `TestClient`, so no server or network is needed. It covers health and model listing, single and batch prediction, request validation (blank, oversized, empty-batch), the metrics counters, and API-key enforcement. These are the tests that guard the serving path described in tour step 13.

sections.title: Optional-dependency skip and client
sections.explanation: `pytest.importorskip` for `fastapi` and `slowapi` skips this module cleanly in environments without them, so the rest of the suite still runs. The repo root is added to `sys.path` so `api.main` can be imported. A single module-level `TestClient(app)` drives the ASGI app directly, which makes the tests fast and deterministic.

sections.title: Health, models and prediction
sections.explanation: These tests check the response contract: `/health` returns `status: ok` and a list of models, and `/models` returns a `models` key. `/predict` returns one of the three labels, echoes the model used, and adds an `X-Process-Time-ms` header, which shows that the timing middleware runs.

sections.title: Input validation
sections.explanation: Whitespace-only text, a 6,000-character string and an empty batch must all return 422. That shows the Pydantic schema enforces non-blank text, a maximum length and a minimum batch size before any model code runs, which protects the service from abusive or malformed input. The batch test also checks that `count` matches the number of results.

sections.title: Metrics counters
sections.explanation: The test first sends a prediction so the counters are not empty, then checks that `/metrics` reports `predictions_total >= 1`. Using `>=` keeps the test independent of test order, because the module-level client shares counter state across tests.

sections.title: API-key enforcement
sections.explanation: `monkeypatch.setenv` sets `FINSIGHT_API_KEY` only for this test. A request without the header must get 401 and one with the correct `X-API-Key` must get 200, which proves the key is read at request time rather than at import. The last test checks that `/health` reports `auth_enabled` and `rate_limit_backend`, so operators can see the security configuration.

tests/test_llm_sentiment.py.overview: This file tests the LLM sentiment benchmark without calling OpenAI. A `StubRunnable` imitates `ChatOpenAI.with_structured_output(..., include_raw=True)` and returns fixed labels, token usage, parse errors and simulated rate-limit failures. The tests cover prompt construction, few-shot leakage, ordering under concurrency, the answer cache, cost accounting and the shared macro-F1 and bootstrap statistics. This answers the interview question of how to test paid, non-deterministic LLM code (tour step 13).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The file imports the public pieces of `llm_sentiment` (labels, system prompt, cache, message builder, classifier, few-shot selector, usage summary) and the shared `stats` functions. Importing the prompt constant lets the tests assert exact prompt structure without copying the text.

sections.title: StubRunnable test double
sections.explanation: The stub copies the real runnable's `invoke` contract: it removes the `Headline: ` prefix from the last message, looks up a predefined answer, and returns a dict with `raw` (holding `usage_metadata`), `parsed` and `parsing_error`. It raises for headlines in `fail_on`, to simulate a rate limit, and it counts calls so tests can check caching. With this stub, labels, token counts and failures are fully deterministic and cost nothing.

sections.title: Prompt construction tests
sections.explanation: Zero-shot prompts must be exactly the system prompt plus one human turn. The few-shot test checks that examples are balanced (two per label) and that none of them appears in the real-news evaluation CSV, which guards against test-set leakage into the prompt. It also checks the message count (system + 2 per example + query). An unknown mode such as chain-of-thought must raise `ValueError`.

sections.title: Classification order and errors
sections.explanation: With `max_concurrency=2`, results must still come back in input order. A valid answer, an unparseable answer and an exception are each recorded differently: a label, `None` with the parse error, and `None` with the exception text. Failures become data instead of crashing a long benchmark run.

sections.title: Answer cache behaviour
sections.explanation: The stub's call counter shows that a second run over the same inputs makes no new API calls and marks every record `cached`. Changing the model name creates a new cache key. Invalid answers are deliberately not cached, so a transient bad output is retried rather than stored forever. This is how the project avoids paying twice for the same benchmark.

sections.title: Usage, cost and statistics
sections.explanation: `summarize_usage` must report cost only when prices are given, rather than inventing a number. It must compute cost per 1k calls and median latency, and count invalid answers and errors. The statistics tests confirm that an invalid prediction (-1) lowers macro-F1, meaning it counts as wrong, and that the bootstrap CI contains the point estimate and reports `n`.

tests/test_rag_news.py.overview: test_rag_news.py tests the retrieval-augmented news Q&A pipeline offline. It uses LangChain's `DeterministicFakeEmbedding` and a `StubAnswer` chat model, so no API keys are needed. The tests cover stable corpus IDs, retrieval ranking, on-disk index caching, prompt numbering with a defence against prompt injection, removal of invented citations, skipping the LLM when nothing is retrieved, and the local TF-IDF/LSA embedding fallback (tour step 13).

sections.title: Imports and fixtures
sections.explanation: The module skips itself if `langchain_core` is missing. The `corpus` fixture is a four-headline DataFrame; one headline is an adversarial instruction meant to test that retrieved text is treated as data. `StubAnswer` records the messages it receives and returns a fixed answer and citation list. A test can therefore check both what the model was asked and how the output is post-processed.

sections.title: Corpus and retrieval tests
sections.explanation: The real corpus must have 2,388 rows with stable integer IDs, so citations stay meaningful across runs. Querying an exact headline must return it first with similarity of about 1.0, and hits must be numbered 1..k. The index test checks that embeddings are saved to a file named after the model and corpus and reloaded on the next build, and that a different corpus produces a separate cache file. Stale indexes cannot be reused by mistake.

sections.title: Prompt and citation safeguards
sections.explanation: The system message must tell the model to ignore instructions found inside sources, and sources must be numbered `[n]` with the question last. Citations to sources that do not exist (for example `[7]` when only two were given) are removed and reported in `dropped_citations`. When no sources are retrieved, the pipeline returns `NOT_FOUND` without calling the LLM, and an empty question raises `ValueError`. Together these tests guard against hallucinated citations and needless paid calls.

sections.title: Sentiment mix and local embeddings
sections.explanation: `sentiment_mix` must return proportions that sum to one, and all zeros for an empty list. The last test checks that the default embedding kind is the local TF-IDF + LSA model and that it actually retrieves on-topic headlines for queries about oil and `$AAPL`. The no-key fallback is therefore usable, not just a placeholder.

tests/test_page_imports.py.overview: test_page_imports.py is a static smoke test for the Streamlit dashboard. It parses every page with Python's `ast` module, finds `from <project module> import ...` statements, and checks that each imported name exists in that module, all without starting Streamlit. It was added after a real bug (importing a symbol that never existed) and catches broken pages in CI (tour step 13).

sections.title: Rationale and setup
sections.explanation: The docstring names the bug it prevents. `PROJECT_MODULES` is every `src/*.py` stem plus the app helpers `shared` and `ui`, so imports from third-party packages are ignored. `PAGE_FILES` is built from every file in `app/views` plus the router, home and shared modules. A new page is therefore covered automatically.

sections.title: AST import extraction
sections.explanation: `_project_imports` walks the syntax tree rather than importing the page. A Streamlit page runs its UI code at import time, so importing it would execute that code. The function yields only `ImportFrom` nodes whose module is a project module, and skips star imports because they have no names to check.

sections.title: Parametrized resolution check
sections.explanation: The test runs once per page (with the page's file name as its ID) and imports each referenced project module for real. A `ModuleNotFoundError` caused by an optional heavy dependency such as torch or shap skips that module instead of failing, so the slim CI environment stays green. The test collects every missing name before asserting, which makes failures easy to act on.

tests/conftest.py.overview: conftest.py holds shared pytest fixtures for the suite: it puts `src/` on `sys.path`, provides small sets of sample positive, negative and neutral financial sentences, and provides project and models directory paths. pytest discovers it automatically, so every test module gets these without importing them (tour step 13).

sections.title: Path setup
sections.explanation: Inserting `src/` into `sys.path` at collection time lets tests write `import preprocess` or `from predict import ...` without packaging the project. This matches how the scripts and the Streamlit app import the same modules.

sections.title: Sample text fixtures
sections.explanation: Three fixtures return short, clearly labelled financial sentences for each class. `mixed_texts` composes them by requesting the other fixtures as parameters, which is pytest's dependency injection. Small hand-written examples keep the model tests readable and quick while still checking each class.

sections.title: Path fixtures
sections.explanation: `project_root` and `models_dir` give tests a single definition of where artifacts live, derived from the file's own location rather than the current working directory. Tests therefore pass no matter where pytest is launched from.

.github/workflows/ci.yml.overview: ci.yml is the continuous-integration workflow. On every push or pull request to main or master it installs the slim `requirements-ci.txt`, runs Ruff lint and format checks across src, app, api and tests, type-checks two core modules with mypy, and runs the pytest suite. Leaving torch and other heavy ML dependencies out of CI keeps it fast, and the tests skip the parts that need them (tour step 14).

sections.title: Triggers
sections.explanation: The workflow runs on pushes and pull requests targeting `main` or `master`. Both branch names are listed so it works whichever default the repository uses. Pull-request runs mean problems are caught before merge, not after.

sections.title: Job and environment setup
sections.explanation: A single `lint-and-test` job runs on Ubuntu with a Python version matrix that currently holds only 3.10, so more versions can be added later. It installs from `requirements-ci.txt` rather than the full requirements. This is the main speed decision: no torch or transformers download. It works because the tests use `importorskip` and tolerate missing modules.

sections.title: Lint, format and type checks
sections.explanation: `ruff check` enforces lint rules and `ruff format --check` fails on unformatted code without rewriting it. mypy runs only on `utils.py` and `preprocess.py` with `--ignore-missing-imports`. The two most-depended-on modules are type-checked strictly, and the rest of the code is not held to the same bar yet.

sections.title: Test run
sections.explanation: The step runs the whole suite verbosely with short tracebacks, which keeps CI logs readable. This includes the offline API, LLM, RAG and page-import tests from step 13.

.github/workflows/retrain.yml.overview: retrain.yml is the scheduled retraining workflow. It runs at 05:00 UTC on the 1st of each month, or on demand, retrains through scripts/retrain.py, runs the test suite, and uploads the regenerated results, registry and joblib models as a 14-day artifact. It deliberately does not commit or deploy them: a human reviews the new metrics first, which prevents a regressed model from shipping silently (tour step 14).

sections.title: Schedule and manual trigger
sections.explanation: The cron expression `0 5 1 * *` means minute 0, hour 5, day 1 of every month. `workflow_dispatch` adds a "Run workflow" button so a retrain can also be started by hand, for example after new data arrives.

sections.title: Setup
sections.explanation: The job checks out the code and installs the same slim CI requirements on Python 3.10. The retrained baselines are scikit-learn TF-IDF models, so no GPU or torch is needed, which keeps a monthly run cheap.

sections.title: Retrain then test
sections.explanation: `scripts/retrain.py` runs training, cross-validation, evaluation and the registry refresh. The test suite then runs against the newly written artifacts, so a retrain that breaks loading or the API contract fails the workflow.

sections.title: Upload artifacts for review
sections.explanation: `actions/upload-artifact` packages `results/`, `models/registry.json` and the `.joblib` models, and keeps them for 14 days. Nothing is pushed back to the repository. A human compares the new metrics with the current ones and commits only if the model has not regressed, which is a human-in-the-loop release gate.

scripts/retrain.py.overview: retrain.py orchestrates the full reproducible pipeline: train the baselines and ensemble, run 5-fold cross-validation, evaluate on the test set, and refresh the model registry. Each step runs the project's existing CLI entry points as a subprocess, so the script is a thin, auditable wrapper rather than a second implementation of the pipeline. The monthly retrain.yml workflow calls it (tour step 14).

sections.title: Docstring and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the four steps and the CLI flags. `ROOT` is resolved from the file's location, and `PY = sys.executable` ensures every subprocess uses the same interpreter and virtual environment as the orchestrator. This avoids "wrong python" bugs in CI.

sections.title: run_step helper
sections.explanation: Each step prints a banner, runs `[python, *args]` with `cwd=ROOT`, and times it. A non-zero exit code raises `SystemExit` with the step name, so the pipeline stops at the first failure (fail fast) and the CI job turns red. Later steps never run on stale or partial outputs.

sections.title: Pipeline in main
sections.explanation: argparse offers `--skip-cv` for faster runs and `--mlflow` to also log the registry to MLflow. The steps call `src/train.py --model baselines`, `src/train.py --model cv`, `src/evaluate.py --save` and `src/registry.py --update` in dependency order. The closing message tells the operator to review results and the registry before committing, which matches the workflow's choice not to auto-commit.

requirements-ci.txt.overview: The slim dependency list installed by the GitHub Actions CI and scheduled-retraining workflows. It deliberately leaves out torch and transformers, so CI can lint, type-check, run the tests and retrain the classical models quickly. Its exact version pins are the main thing to understand: the committed models are pickled artifacts, so the training libraries in CI must match the versions they were saved with. It belongs to tour step 14 (CI/CD and Retraining).

sections.title: Why exact pins matter
sections.explanation: The header comment explains the design. `models/*.joblib` files are pickled scikit-learn objects, and pickles are only reliably loadable by the same library version that wrote them. If an unpinned install pulled pandas 3 or a newer scikit-learn, unpickling and label encoding would break. In an interview this is a good, concrete example of reproducibility in ML systems: the model artifact and its runtime environment have to be versioned together.

sections.title: Core ML and data stack
sections.explanation: These are pinned with `==` versions of scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, scipy and joblib, which is what training, evaluation and model loading need. It also pins matplotlib (evaluation plots), `datasets` (Hugging Face dataset loading), tqdm and PyYAML. Pinning everything here, not just scikit-learn, avoids a transitive upgrade (for example numpy) quietly changing behavior between CI runs.

sections.title: API test dependencies
sections.explanation: FastAPI, uvicorn, slowapi (rate limiting) and httpx (used by FastAPI's TestClient) let CI exercise the inference API in-process. These use lower bounds (`>=`) instead of exact pins because they do not affect pickled artifacts, so a compatible newer release is acceptable.

sections.title: LLM and tooling extras
sections.explanation: The LangChain packages are pinned so the LLM benchmark and news Q&A code can be imported and tested. The comment notes they only make real calls when an Anthropic or OpenAI API key is present, so tests can run without one. The last group (pytest, ruff, mypy) holds the quality gates that ci.yml runs: tests, lint/format checks and static type checking.

docker-compose.yml.overview: Defines the multi-container deployment: a Streamlit UI, an nginx load balancer, horizontally scalable FastAPI replicas, and a shared Redis instance. The header comment gives the run command (`docker compose up --build --scale api=3`) and the exposed ports. This file is the center of tour step 15 (Containerized Deployment) and shows the split-architecture idea that the UI and the model-serving tier scale independently.

sections.title: Architecture header
sections.explanation: The comment describes the request path: UI, then the nginx load balancer, then N FastAPI replicas, with Redis shared for rate limiting. It also documents the two public entry points: port 8501 for the UI and port 8080 for the load-balanced API. Writing the topology at the top makes the file explain itself to anyone running it.

sections.title: Redis shared state
sections.explanation: Redis runs from the small `redis:7-alpine` image and uses `expose`, not `ports`, so it is reachable only on the internal compose network and never from the host. It exists because each API replica would otherwise keep its own in-memory rate-limit counters, and a client could get N times the limit by being spread across N replicas. Moving the counters into one shared store keeps the API replicas stateless.

sections.title: Scalable API service
sections.explanation: The API is built from `Dockerfile.api` and configured through environment variables. `FINSIGHT_API_KEY` defaults to empty through `${VAR:-}` syntax, which gives an open demo unless a key is set. `FINSIGHT_REDIS_URL` uses the service name `redis` as the hostname (compose DNS), and `FINSIGHT_TRUST_PROXY=true` tells the API to trust forwarded client-IP headers from nginx. Only port 8000 is exposed internally and no host port is published, which is what lets `--scale api=N` run many replicas without port conflicts.

sections.title: nginx load balancer
sections.explanation: The stock `nginx:alpine` image is used with the project's config mounted read-only (`:ro`) over the default nginx.conf, so no custom image needs to be built. It publishes host port 8080 to container port 80, which makes it the single public front door for the API tier. Note that `depends_on` only controls start order, not readiness. The API's own HEALTHCHECK covers whether it is ready.

sections.title: Streamlit UI service
sections.explanation: The UI is built from the main `Dockerfile` and pointed at `http://lb:80` through `FINSIGHT_API_URL`. Predictions therefore go through the load balancer to the API tier instead of running inside the UI process. It passes the same API key so its requests are authorized. This separation lets you scale the compute-heavy model tier without duplicating the UI, a likely interview talking point.

Dockerfile.api.overview: Builds the image for the FastAPI inference service that docker-compose scales into replicas. It is a lean image: CPU-only PyTorch, the deploy requirements plus the redis client, and only the `src/`, `api/` and `models/` directories. It adds a health check and runs uvicorn with two workers. It is part of tour step 15 (Containerized Deployment).

sections.title: Base image and environment
sections.explanation: It starts from `python:3.10-slim` to keep the base small. `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` makes logs show up immediately in `docker logs`, and `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR` stops pip from keeping caches in the layer. `HF_HOME` fixes where Hugging Face downloads models (for example FinBERT) inside the container, and `TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY=error` quiets library log noise.

sections.title: System and Python dependencies
sections.explanation: `build-essential` is installed so packages that compile native code can build, and the apt lists are removed in the same RUN to keep the layer small. Torch is installed first from the CPU-only wheel index: the default CUDA wheel is several gigabytes and serving does not need a GPU. When requirements-deploy.txt is installed afterwards, its torch requirement is already met. `redis` is added here only for the API image because only the API tier talks to Redis. Copying the requirements file before the source code means Docker can cache these slow layers across code-only changes.

sections.title: Minimal application copy
sections.explanation: Only the model code (`src/`), the API (`api/`) and the trained artifacts (`models/`) are copied. The UI, the data and the extension datasets are left out on purpose, which keeps the image smaller and reduces what the serving tier exposes. Baking the models into the image makes each replica self-contained and immutable: a new model version means a new image.

sections.title: Health check and startup
sections.explanation: The HEALTHCHECK calls `/health` with Python's standard-library urllib, because the slim image has no curl. The 10-second start period allows time for the models to load. uvicorn binds `0.0.0.0` so it can be reached from other containers, and it runs `--workers 2`. That gives two levels of scaling: processes inside each replica, and replicas added by the orchestrator, as the comment says.

deploy/nginx.conf.overview: The nginx configuration for the load balancer in front of the scaled FastAPI replicas. It does two non-obvious things: it re-resolves the `api` service name through Docker's DNS so new replicas receive traffic, and it forwards the real client IP so the API's rate limiter counts per caller, not per proxy. It is mounted read-only into the `lb` service in docker-compose and belongs to tour step 15.

sections.title: Docker DNS resolver
sections.explanation: `127.0.0.11` is Docker's embedded DNS server. With a plain `proxy_pass http://api:8000`, nginx resolves the name once at startup and can stay pinned to whatever addresses it saw then. Declaring a `resolver` with `valid=10s` and using a variable in `proxy_pass` (below) makes nginx look the name up again at request time. Docker DNS returns the addresses of all replicas, so traffic spreads across replicas created with `--scale`. `ipv6=off` avoids lookups for AAAA records the compose network does not provide.

sections.title: Logging to container streams
sections.explanation: Access logs go to stdout and errors (warn level and above) go to stderr. This follows the container convention of logging to standard streams so `docker logs` or a log collector picks them up, and no log files build up inside the container.

sections.title: Forwarded client headers
sections.explanation: The server listens on port 80 inside the container (mapped to 8080 on the host). Without these headers, every request would seem to come from nginx's own IP, and the per-IP rate limiter would put all users in one bucket. `X-Real-IP` and `X-Forwarded-For` carry the original caller's address, which the API trusts only because `FINSIGHT_TRUST_PROXY=true` is set. That opt-in matters because forwarded headers are easy to fake when there is no trusted proxy in front.

sections.title: Dynamic upstream proxying
sections.explanation: `set $api_upstream` and then `proxy_pass $api_upstream` is the variable trick that triggers the per-request DNS lookup described at the top. The short 5-second connect timeout fails fast when a replica is unreachable. The 60-second read timeout leaves room for slower inference requests, such as transformer-model predictions on CPU.

Dockerfile.overview: Builds the Streamlit dashboard image, the `ui` service in docker-compose. It uses the same lean base and CPU-only PyTorch approach as the API image, but copies more: the app, the data, the Streamlit config and the nested stock-prediction extension that some dashboard pages need. It finishes with a Streamlit health check and a headless launch on port 8501. It is part of tour step 15 (Containerized Deployment).

sections.title: Base image and environment
sections.explanation: This is the same `python:3.10-slim` base and environment setup as Dockerfile.api: unbuffered output for live logs, no pip cache, a fixed Hugging Face cache path and quieter transformers logging. Keeping the two images consistent makes them easier to reason about and maintain.

sections.title: Dependency installation
sections.explanation: It installs build tools and cleans the apt lists in the same layer, then installs CPU-only torch before the rest of requirements-deploy.txt. The comment notes that the torch line in the requirements file then does nothing because torch is already installed. That ordering is how the image avoids the large CUDA build. Unlike the API image, it does not add the redis client, because the UI never talks to Redis.

sections.title: Application and data copy
sections.explanation: The UI image copies `app/` and `.streamlit/` (theme and server config), plus `src/`, `models/` and `data/`. The dashboard pages read datasets and can still load models locally, so they need more files than the API tier does. This is why the UI image is heavier than Dockerfile.api, even though in the compose setup predictions are routed to the API.

sections.title: Stock-prediction extension
sections.explanation: Only the `src/`, `data/` and `models/` folders of the nested external project are copied, and the comment says virtualenvs are excluded. Copying selected subfolders instead of the whole directory keeps local environments and other unrelated files out of the image. The comment names the consumers (`app/views/9_Stock_Prediction_Extension.py` and `src/stock_extension.py`), which documents why this cross-project copy exists.

sections.title: Health check and entrypoint
sections.explanation: Port 8501 is exposed, and the HEALTHCHECK calls Streamlit's built-in `/_stcore/health` endpoint with stdlib urllib, since curl is not installed in slim images. The ENTRYPOINT runs Streamlit bound to `0.0.0.0` so it can be reached from outside the container, and `--server.headless=true` stops it from trying to open a browser or show interactive prompts.

app/shared.py.overview: Thin compatibility/barrel layer that re-exports the design-system tokens and components from ui.py under one import surface for all pages, preserving historical names like inject_css and create_probability_chart.

app/views/2_Batch_Processing.py.overview: Batch processing page implementing an upload, validate, preview, analyze, summarize, export flow for CSV/text inputs, with aggregate sentiment KPIs, distribution charts, an LLM market-outlook summary and downloadable results.

app/views/4_Word_Insights.py.overview: Word Insights page visualising the vocabulary each TF-IDF baseline model weights most heavily per sentiment class, as bar charts and term tables.

app/views/5_Deep_Analysis.py.overview: Deep Analysis page running advanced rule-based NLP (Loughran-McDonald lexicon, entity extraction, linguistic measurements) and a deterministic chain-of-thought reasoning trace alongside the model verdict.

app/views/6_Model_Info.py.overview: Model registry page showing the selected model's PhraseBank test metrics (n=226), 5-fold cross-validation results, interval charts comparing models and a per-class breakdown, all read from saved result artifacts.

app/views/8_Error_Analysis.py.overview: Error analysis page that re-runs a baseline model on a data split, builds a per-sentence correctness/confidence table, and surfaces confusion patterns, confident mistakes and model weaknesses.

app/views/9_Stock_Prediction_Extension.p.overview: Experimental Labs page that drives the nested stock-prediction workflow (price download, live news fetch, FinBERT scoring, feature engineering, LSTM training, next-day direction prediction) and charts price/sentiment timelines with the headlines used.

src/benchmark_finbert.py.overview: Script that benchmarks the off-the-shelf ProsusAI FinBERT model on the same held-out PhraseBank test split as the baselines and appends accuracy/F1/precision/recall to results/evaluation_results.json, so the README comparison table covers every claimed model on equal footing.

src/integrate_news.py.overview: Cross-dataset integration: scores news headlines with a trained model, aggregates them into daily per-ticker sentiment, correlates sentiment with stock returns, feeds the Streamlit trends page, and measures true out-of-distribution generalization on the real, human-labeled zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment set. Explicitly flags the bundled sample_news.csv as synthetic so correlation results are not over-claimed.

src/stock_extension.py.overview: Bridge into the nested financial-news-stock-prediction sub-project: loads its data collection, feature engineering, FinBERT sentiment and LSTM components, fetches prices and news (with sample-news and neutral-sentiment fallbacks), aligns daily sentiment to prices, trains an LSTM, predicts next-day movement, and returns a structured result dataclass. Also exposes a CLI.

.dockerignore.overview: Docker build-context exclusion list that keeps virtualenvs, git history, caches, notebooks, tests, docs and the nested project's scratch/venv folders out of the image, shrinking the context and preventing local artifacts leaking into containers.

Makefile.overview: Windows-oriented developer task runner with targets for venv install, launching the Streamlit dashboard, running pytest, ruff + mypy linting, ruff formatting, cache cleanup, and killing stale Streamlit processes via a PowerShell script.

PRODUCT.md.overview: Product brief for the FinSight dashboard defining its two audiences (finance analysts and technical evaluators), its honest-evaluation positioning (SVM 0.90 in-domain F1 collapsing to 0.46 OOD, recovered to 0.84 by news-fine-tuned FinBERT), operating context, model and page inventory, product principles and accessibility commitments. Serves as the design-system brief for UI work.

pyproject.toml.overview: Project metadata (Python >=3.10) and central tool configuration: lenient mypy settings, pytest discovery rooted at tests/ with verbose short tracebacks, and ruff lint (E/F/W/I, line length 120) and format rules.

requirements-deploy.txt.overview: Full-featured deployment dependency set with lower-bound version ranges supporting all dashboard pages (FinBERT, LSTM extension), the FastAPI inference API, LangChain LLM features, SHAP and yfinance; torch is left unpinned because the Dockerfiles install a CPU-only build first.

requirements-full.txt.overview: Frozen pip-freeze-style lockfile of the full transitive environment (~89 packages, e.g. streamlit 1.55, transformers 5.3, scikit-learn 1.7.2) used to reproduce an exact working environment.

requirements.txt.overview: Primary install requirements for local development and Streamlit Community Cloud, adding the PyTorch CPU extra index to avoid the ~2 GB CUDA wheel exceeding free-tier build limits; pins core ML, Streamlit, LangChain, SHAP and data-loading packages.

docs/APP_FLOW.md.overview: Describes the Streamlit dashboard's user journeys (single analysis, batch, explainability, trends/error analysis, stock extension), page order, and shared runtime behavior such as cached model loading and graceful degradation of optional modules.

docs/DESIGN.md.overview: FinSight design system spec with YAML front-matter tokens (colours, typography) and prose rules framing the dashboard as a central bank 'Inflation Report': white report ground, teal shell, hairline rules, numbered exhibits, uncertainty bands, and triple-coded sentiment (colour, glyph, word).

docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md.overview: Six-phase implementation plan covering repo stabilization, ML flow validation, dashboard validation, trust/honesty improvements, deployment choices (Streamlit Cloud vs Docker hosts), and UI polish.

docs/PRODUCTION_SETUP.md.overview: Operations guide for local setup, running the Streamlit app and training/evaluation scripts, Docker build/run, Streamlit Cloud and Render/Railway/Fly.io deployment, and a production readiness checklist.

docs/README.md.overview: Index of the docs folder plus a project overview: model variants, evaluation features, core stack, repository layout, main use cases, and honesty notes about FinBERT and rule-based reasoning.

docs/RETRAINING.md.overview: Retraining guide describing the automated orchestrator (scripts/retrain.py), the monthly scheduled CI workflow that uploads artifacts without auto-committing weights, a manual checklist with a macro-F1 regression guardrail, and model promotion criteria.

docs/RULES.md.overview: Project rules across product, data, model, UI, engineering, deployment, and resume honesty: no overclaiming, no test leakage, deterministic splits, report macro-F1, cache heavy loads, and keep docs in sync with code.

docs/TRACKER.md.overview: Epic-based progress tracker listing completed and pending work: core sentiment system, explainability, dashboard pages, quality/CI, deployment hardening, FastAPI service and MLOps, UX, and the LangChain/Claude LLM layer (benchmark, RAG).

docs/TRD.md.overview: Technical requirements document listing system components, runtime dependencies, data requirements, technical constraints (cached loading, isolated baseline/transformer paths, root-aware paths), non-functional requirements, and engineering standards.

.streamlit/config.toml.overview: Streamlit theme configuration for the FinSight dashboard: a light 'central-bank report' palette with WCAG AA contrast, custom chart colour scales, and self-hosted Public Sans font faces.

api/__init__.py.overview: Package marker that makes api/ an importable Python package so tests and uvicorn can load api.main.

app/static/fonts/PublicSans-LICENSE.txt.overview: SIL Open Font License 1.1 text covering the self-hosted Public Sans font files shipped with the Streamlit dashboard.

scripts/kill_streamlit.ps1.overview: Windows PowerShell utility that finds processes holding port 8501 or running Streamlit and terminates them so the dashboard can restart cleanly.

src/llm_enhanced.py.overview: Rule-based 'chain-of-thought' explanation engine that walks a text through comprehension, entity extraction, sentiment detection, context analysis, confidence calibration and synthesis steps, producing traceable reasoning, comprehensive explanations and market-outlook narratives without any external LLM API.

src/llm_explain.py.overview: Template-based natural-language explanation generator that turns model word-importance scores into readable prediction explanations and market outlooks, with no external LLM required.

src/nlp_advanced.py.overview: Advanced financial text processing: cleaning, normalisation, tokenisation and feature extraction (lexicon counts, negations, numbers) plus a lexicon-based FinancialTextAnalyzer that scores sentiment with calibrated confidence, batch analysis and aggregation.

tests/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker for the tests directory.

tests/test_api_client.py.overview: Unit tests for RemotePredictor with httpx.post monkeypatched, covering single and batch prediction, error-status and connection-failure handling, and the empty fallback of remote_available_models.

tests/test_integrate_news.py.overview: Pytest suite for integrate_news.py covering news headline and stock data loading, news sentiment prediction, daily sentiment aggregation and sentiment trend computation across datasets.

tests/test_llm_enhanced.py.overview: Unit tests for the rule-based reasoning layer in llm_enhanced.py: chain-of-thought sentiment reasoner outputs (valid label, confidence range, reasoning trace, key factors), explanation generator modes, bullish/bearish market outlook and ThoughtStep serialization.

tests/test_llm_provider.py.overview: Tests for the LangChain provider abstraction in llm_provider.py: Claude is the default provider, provider is inferred from whichever API key is set, OpenAI/OpenRouter require an explicit model, unknown providers are rejected, temperature can be omitted, and chat clients build offline without calling the API.

tests/test_nlp_advanced.py.overview: Unit tests for nlp_advanced.py and the financial lexicons: text cleaning/normalization and feature extraction (negation, polarity word counts), FinancialTextAnalyzer single/batch/aggregate analysis, company/ticker extraction that avoids fragmenting words or matching currency codes, and lexicon coverage.

tests/test_predict.py.overview: Tests for predict.py: model discovery via get_available_models and SentimentPredictor single/batch prediction, probability outputs and confidence range.

tests/test_preprocess.py.overview: Unit tests for preprocess.py: text cleaning (lowercasing, whitespace, special characters), DataFrame preprocessing with label encoding and empty-row dropping, and train/val/test split sizes with no overlap (leakage check).

tests/test_shap_explain.py.overview: Tests for shap_explain.py: SHAP availability, explanations for gradient boosting and logistic regression baselines, per-class feature contributions, and saving results to JSON. Skips when SHAP or trained models are absent.

tests/test_stock_extension.py.overview: Tests for stock_extension.py using a fully stubbed component map (price download, live/sample news, filtering, sentiment, LSTM). Verifies live-news runs, fallback to sample and market-sample news for any ticker, ticker-specific LSTM model paths and graceful model saving without real torch.

tests/test_utils.py.overview: Unit tests for utils.py: project root and path helpers, idempotent logging setup without duplicate handlers, label map constants and round-trip, classifier/transformer constants, and get_model_info defaults.
